Dimmesdale punishes himself in private with a bloody scourge, fasting and sleepless vigils, while his sermons, fed by his anguish, grow ever more powerful and beloved. One night he climbs the scaffold alone. Hester and Pearl pass by, returning from Governor Winthrop's deathbed, and he calls them up to stand hand in hand with him. Pearl asks if he will stand with them at noon tomorrow; he says not yet. A meteor seems to trace a great A across the sky. Chillingworth watches from below.

Seven years have passed. Hester's quiet charity has softened the town, and many now say her A stands for Able. Yet she sees that Dimmesdale is being destroyed and blames her promise of secrecy. Meeting Chillingworth gathering herbs on the shore, she is shocked by how he has changed: once a mild scholar, he has become a fiend, feeding on another man's pain. He refuses to show mercy, so Hester resolves to break her promise and warn the minister herself.

Hester waits for Dimmesdale on a path through the dark forest and finally tells him the truth: his doctor is her wronged husband. He is horrified and angry, then forgives her. Away from the town's eyes, Hester urges him to flee with her and Pearl to Europe and begin again. He agrees. Hester unfastens the scarlet letter, tosses it beside the brook and lets down her long, rich hair. Sunlight floods the gloomy forest, and for a moment both seem young and free.

cards.q: What we did had a consecration of its own. We felt it so! We said so to each other!
cards.b: Hester says this to Dimmesdale in the forest, at the hinge of the book. It is a startling claim in a Puritan world: that their love, whatever the law called it, was holy to them. For a moment she speaks as a free woman, and it is exactly that freedom that the novel will test.

cards.t: Pearl will not cross the brook
cards.b: Hester calls Pearl over to meet the minister, but the child stops on the far bank of the brook, points at her mother's breast and throws a furious tantrum until Hester picks up the scarlet letter and pins it back on. Only then does Pearl come, and when Dimmesdale kisses her brow, she runs to the brook and washes the kiss away. The plan holds: a ship bound for Bristol leaves in four days, just after Dimmesdale preaches the great Election Day sermon.

Dimmesdale returns to town giddy, tempted to whisper blasphemies to a deacon and a pious widow, and the witch Mistress Hibbins hints she knows where he has been. He burns his old sermon and writes a new one all night. On Election Day, amid crowds, sailors and Native visitors, Hester learns from the ship's captain that Chillingworth has booked passage on the same ship. Then Dimmesdale preaches the most inspired sermon of his life, and the town hails him as a saint.

Leaving the meeting house in triumph, Dimmesdale suddenly falters. He calls Hester and Pearl to him and, leaning on Hester, climbs the scaffold as Chillingworth begs him to stop: there was no place so secret, he cries, that the minister could have escaped him, save this one. Dimmesdale confesses before all Boston that he is Pearl's father and tears open his shirt. Pearl kisses him at last, and her tears break the spell on her. He dies on the scaffold.

Witnesses argue about what they saw: some describe a scarlet A in the minister's flesh, others nothing at all. Robbed of his purpose, Chillingworth withers and dies within a year, leaving his large fortune to Pearl. Hester and Pearl vanish to Europe. Years later Hester returns alone, by her own choice, still wearing the letter, and becomes a counsellor to troubled women. Pearl seems to have married well abroad. Hester is buried near Dimmesdale, beneath one stone marked with a scarlet A.

Hester turns punishment into a kind of art: she embroiders her badge of shame so beautifully that it becomes her own. Proud, passionate and fiercely loyal, she keeps her lover's secret for seven years and raises Pearl alone. Isolation makes her a free and radical thinker, though Hawthorne worries over it. She is one of the first great heroines of American fiction.

Gifted, gentle and admired as a near-saint, Dimmesdale shares Hester's sin but lacks her courage. He hates his hypocrisy yet cannot give up his reputation, so he punishes himself in secret instead. His suffering makes him a better preacher and a worse man. Only when death is near does he find the strength to stand where Hester stood.

A learned, patient scholar, Chillingworth is the most wronged person in the story, and he becomes its worst sinner. Instead of seeking justice, he chooses intimacy with his victim, living beside Dimmesdale as his doctor and feeding on his pain. Hawthorne calls his crime the violation of a human heart. When his prey escapes into confession, he has nothing left.

Three people sin, and each carries it differently. Hester's sin is public, so she can live with it, repent and grow. Dimmesdale's is hidden, so it festers into self-hatred. Chillingworth's is the coldest of all, yet looks like friendship. Hawthorne's verdict is clear: the secret, not the sin itself, does the deepest damage. As the narrator says, be true, show the world something of your worst.

The scarlet A was meant to mean one thing: Adulteress. But the letter keeps shifting. Hester's needlework makes it beautiful, her service makes people read it as Able, the sky seems to write it as Angel for Winthrop, and Dimmesdale carries it hidden on his flesh. Hawthorne shows that symbols do not fix people; people slowly change what symbols mean.

Puritan Boston is a world of iron rules, gray clothes and watching eyes. Against it Hawthorne sets the wild rosebush, the sunlit forest and Pearl herself, untamed and truthful. The forest frees Hester's hair and heart, but the novel does not simply side with nature: Pearl insists on the letter, and lasting peace comes only through honesty within the community.

Hester's punishment is brutal but short, and she builds a life after it. Dimmesdale escapes punishment and spends seven years rotting from within, his hand pressed to his heart. When you've done wrong, the confession you dread is usually lighter than the secret you'd carry. Owning a mistake early limits its power over you.

Chillingworth had every reason to be angry. But by making another man's pain his life's project, he turns into a stooped, shadowy creature, and when Dimmesdale dies he withers within a year. Grudges promise satisfaction and deliver emptiness. If someone has wronged you, guard against letting them become the centre of your life.

Boston gave Hester a single letter meant to define her forever. She didn't argue; she simply lived well, sewing, nursing and helping, until people read the A as Able. When others pin a label on you, steady, generous action over time can change what it means more surely than protest.

The townspeople despise Hester and worship Dimmesdale, though he committed the same sin and lied about it for years. Polished public virtue can hide private failure, and the loudest moralists are not always the most honest. Be slow to condemn and slow to idolize; most people are more complicated than their reputation.

The forest plan to sail to Europe feels like freedom, yet Pearl won't come until the letter is back on, and Chillingworth books passage on the same ship. Changing places does not change what you carry. Real fresh starts begin with facing the truth where you are, as Dimmesdale finally does on the scaffold.

Pearl constantly asks the questions adults avoid: why her mother wears the letter, why the minister holds his hand over his heart, why he won't stand with them by day. Her honesty is uncomfortable, but it pushes everyone toward truth. Listen to the awkward questions children ask; they often point straight at what you're hiding.

The goodwives at the scaffold want Hester branded on the forehead or hanged. Their harshness makes confession terrifying, which is exactly why Dimmesdale stays silent. A family, office or town that punishes every failing teaches people to hide them. Make it safe to admit mistakes, and you'll get more honesty.

Hester wore her mistake openly and grew stronger; Dimmesdale hid his and was hollowed out. Is there something you've been carrying in secret, an error, a regret or a resentment, that might weigh less if you spoke it aloud to someone you trust? What would it take to set it down?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Borrowed dreams make real life unbearable
pts.d: measured against convent-school romances and the Vaubyessard ball, Emma's ordinary marriage looks like failure.

pts.h: Debt is desire with a due date
pts.d: the draper Lheureux's easy credit turns Emma's longings into promissory notes, and the seizure order finally kills her.

pts.h: Clichés are a moral danger, not just bad style
pts.d: at the agricultural fair, Rodolphe's stock phrases seduce Emma precisely because they sound like her novels.

pts.h: The world often rewards the hollow
pts.d: while Emma and Charles die ruined, Homais, the pompous pharmacist, wins the Legion of Honour.

cards.b: Around 1830 a clumsy schoolboy, Charles Bovary, grows into a plodding, good-natured man who scrapes through his exams to become an officier de santé, a second-class country doctor in Tostes, Normandy. This is the July Monarchy: prosperous, money-minded and deeply provincial. His mother marries him to an older widow for her supposed fortune, which proves fictitious; the shock helps kill her. Setting a farmer's broken leg at Les Bertaux, Charles has met the farmer's daughter Emma, pretty and convent-educated. He proposes, and they marry at a huge, boozy two-day country wedding.

Emma had been raised by nuns in Rouen, where she devoured sentimental novels, Walter Scott's romances and pious keepsakes full of moonlit lakes, swooning ladies and gallant knights. She expected marriage to deliver passion, bliss and intoxication, the words she had read about. Instead she gets Charles, who eats contentedly, snores, talks in commonplaces and adores her without noticing her at all. In the narrow house in Tostes she grows restless, walks with her greyhound Djali, and asks herself again and again why on earth she married.

One autumn the Bovarys are invited, thanks to a lucky medical favour, to a ball at the chateau of the Marquis d'Andervilliers. For one night Emma lives inside her dreams: chandeliers, silks, iced champagne and pomegranates, aristocrats murmuring of Italy, and a waltz with a viscount. Riding home, Charles picks up a green silk cigar case dropped on the road, and Emma treasures it as a relic. Afterwards Tostes is unbearable. She sinks into nervous illness, and Charles, worried, gives up his practice and moves them to Yonville-l'Abbaye.

Yonville is a sleepy market town near Rouen, and Flaubert fills it with unforgettable types. Homais the pharmacist is a pompous freethinker who quotes Voltaire and lectures everyone on progress. Lheureux the draper is an oily merchant who lends money as easily as he sells lace. Bournisien the priest is kindly but obtuse; Binet the tax collector turns napkin rings on his lathe. At the inn Emma meets Léon Dupuis, a young law clerk who shares her taste for poetry, music and sunsets. Soon her daughter Berthe is born; Emma had wanted a son.

Emma and Léon fall into a tender, unspoken love, all long glances and talk of books. Léon is too timid to act, and Emma decides to play the perfect wife, glorying in her own sacrifice while secretly resenting Charles more than ever. She meets Lheureux, who begins tempting her with scarves and trinkets. Desperate, she seeks help from Father Bournisien, but he thinks only of bodily ailments and his catechism class and cannot hear what she is saying. Bored and frustrated, Léon leaves Yonville to study law in Paris.

Rodolphe Boulanger, a rich bachelor and practised seducer who owns the estate of La Huchette, brings a servant to Charles for bleeding and sizes Emma up in a single glance: she is gasping for love like a carp for water, he thinks, and will be easy to get rid of afterwards. At the town's agricultural fair he courts her at a window above the crowd, and Flaubert cuts his love talk against the official speeches and prize announcements for manure and pigs. An old servant, Catherine Leroux, receives a medal for fifty-four years of labour.

Charles, eager to please, suggests that riding would be good for Emma's health, and Rodolphe offers to escort her. On a ride through the autumn woods she yields to him. Back home she looks in the mirror and repeats to herself, I have a lover, a lover, as if she had finally entered the novels she loved. The affair grows reckless: she runs across the fields at dawn to his chateau, and they meet at night in the arbour of the Bovarys' own garden while Charles sleeps upstairs.

Homais, hungry for local glory, persuades Charles to operate on the clubfoot of Hippolyte, the stable boy at the inn, using a new surgical technique Charles barely understands. Emma, hoping a triumph will let her admire her husband, encourages him. The operation is a disaster: the leg turns gangrenous and the eminent Doctor Canivet arrives from Neufchâtel to amputate it above the knee. Hippolyte's screams fill the town. Emma's last scrap of respect for Charles dies, and she throws herself back at Rodolphe with redoubled passion and lavish gifts.

Emma showers Rodolphe with presents bought on credit from Lheureux, who is quietly building a pile of promissory notes. She demands that they run away together to Italy with little Berthe, and Rodolphe seems to agree. But he has grown bored with her extravagant declarations, which sound to him like every other mistress he has had. On the eve of their departure he writes a smooth, insincere farewell letter, sprinkling a drop of water on it to pass for a tear, and sends it to her hidden in a basket of apricots.

cards.q: Human speech is like a cracked tin kettle, on which we hammer out tunes to make bears dance when we long to move the stars.
cards.b: Flaubert writes this at the hinge of the novel, as Rodolphe dismisses Emma's sincere words because they sound like clichés. It is his own confession too: a writer who agonised for days over a single sentence. Everyone in the book reaches for borrowed language, and nobody quite manages to say what they truly feel.

cards.t: Collapse and the opera at Rouen
cards.b: Reading the letter in the attic, Emma nearly throws herself from the window. She falls into a brain fever that lasts for weeks, then a spell of extravagant piety. To cheer her, Charles takes her to the opera in Rouen to hear Lucia di Lammermoor, and there they run into Léon, back from Paris and grown bolder. Charles suggests Emma stay on an extra day. Léon takes her on a famous cab ride: the coach rattles round and round Rouen for hours with its blinds drawn, while the scandalised driver wonders why nobody gets out.

Emma becomes Léon's mistress. Inventing piano lessons with a teacher called Mademoiselle Lempereur, she travels to Rouen every Thursday and spends the day with him in a room at the Hôtel de Boulogne. She persuades Charles to give her power of attorney over a small inheritance, and Lheureux helps her squander it. The affair repeats the pattern of her marriage: the thrill fades, Léon grows nervous about his career and his reputation, and Emma, Flaubert writes, finds in adultery all the platitudes of marriage. She lies constantly and spends wildly.

Lheureux, who has been renewing her notes at ruinous interest, finally calls them in. A court orders the Bovarys' furniture seized for eight thousand francs, and the bailiff inventories the house. Emma runs to everyone. Léon cannot find the money and flinches when she hints he should steal it. Guillaumin the notary offers help in exchange for her body, and she refuses him in disgust. She even goes to Binet. At last she goes to La Huchette and begs Rodolphe, who coolly says he has no money while standing among his expensive things.

Half mad with despair, Emma hurries to the pharmacy, gets the key to Homais's storeroom from his young assistant Justin, who adores her, and eats a handful of arsenic straight from the jar. Her death is long and horribly physical: vomiting, convulsions, a black tongue. Charles and the doctors are helpless. Bournisien gives her the last rites, and as she dies she hears a blind beggar from the Rouen road singing a bawdy song beneath the window. She laughs a dreadful, frantic laugh, and then she is gone.

Charles, crushed, pays her debts and spoils her grave. Then he finds her letters from Léon and Rodolphe and learns everything. Meeting Rodolphe at the market, he says he bears no grudge: it is the fault of fatality. Soon afterwards he is found dead on a garden bench, holding a lock of Emma's hair. Little Berthe, penniless, is sent to a poor aunt and ends up working in a cotton mill. Homais, meanwhile, crushes his rivals, flatters the authorities and, in the novel's last line, receives the Legion of Honour.

cards.t: Emma Bovary: the reader who drowns
cards.b: Emma is vain, selfish and reckless, yet she is the only person in Yonville who wants more than food and status. Her tragedy is that she can imagine longing only in the clichés she has been fed, so every real man and every real day disappoints her. Flaubert said, perhaps, Madame Bovary, c'est moi: he mocks her, but he knows her from the inside.

cards.t: Charles Bovary: the loyal blind man
cards.b: Charles is mediocre, slow and smug, and also the most faithful person in the novel. He loves Emma completely and never sees her at all. His goodness is real but useless, because it has no imagination in it. His end, dying on a bench with her hair in his hand, is the book's most quietly devastating image.

cards.t: Homais: the triumph of the windbag
cards.b: The pharmacist is Flaubert's portrait of bourgeois stupidity dressed up as enlightenment. Homais spouts slogans about science and progress, pushes Charles into the botched operation, practises medicine illegally and gets a rival doctor driven out. He never suffers, never doubts and never learns, and the novel ends with the state pinning a medal on his chest.

Emma's mind is furnished by novels, keepsakes and operas; her life is furnished by Charles's dinners and Yonville's gossip. The gap between them is the engine of the book. The French even coined a word from her, bovarysme: the habit of imagining yourself as someone other than you are, and despising the life you actually have.

cards.t: Money and the market in desire
cards.b: Every one of Emma's dreams has a price tag, and Lheureux is always there with credit. Shawls, riding crops, a gold-topped cane for Rodolphe, the hotel room in Rouen: love and luxury are bought on the same notes. Flaubert shows a new commercial world that sells people fantasies and then collects, with interest, on their ruin.

Flaubert hated received ideas, and here everyone speaks in them: Homais in slogans of progress, Rodolphe in stock phrases of love, the officials at the fair in empty patriotism. Emma is seduced by language she has already read. The novel's cool, exact style, with no moralising narrator, is itself Flaubert's protest against easy words.

cards.t: Don't compare your life to a story
cards.b: Emma judges her marriage against novels and one glittering night at La Vaubyessard, and real life cannot compete. Comparing your ordinary days with someone else's highlights, on a page or a screen, guarantees disappointment. Ask what your actual life offers, rather than what it lacks next to an edited fantasy.

Lheureux never pressures Emma; he simply makes buying effortless and paying later feel painless. Each small note seems harmless until they are all called in at once and the bailiff is in her parlour. Be wary of anyone who is eager to lend you money, and add up the real cost before you sign.

cards.t: Smooth words can be the least sincere
cards.b: Rodolphe's lines at the agricultural fair and his farewell letter with its fake tear are polished precisely because he feels nothing. Emma's clumsy, gushing sincerity sounds false to him. Judge people by what they do when it costs them something, as Rodolphe's refusal of help at La Huchette finally shows, not by how well they talk.

cards.t: A new thrill does not cure an old emptiness
cards.b: Emma flees boredom with Rodolphe, then with Léon, and in Rouen discovers the same flatness she felt with Charles. Changing the person, the town or the purchase did not change her. When restlessness keeps returning whatever you do, the answer is more likely inside you than in the next adventure.

cards.t: Don't gamble other people's safety for glory
cards.b: Homais and Charles operate on Hippolyte's foot to win fame, not because the stable boy needed it, and Hippolyte loses his leg. Ambition that experiments on someone else's body or livelihood is reckless however modern it sounds. Before you take a risk, ask who actually pays if it goes wrong.

Charles loves Emma devotedly yet never notices her misery, her debts or her lies. Good intentions without curiosity can leave the people closest to us utterly alone. Real care means asking questions and listening to the answers, even when they are unwelcome, as Charles never once did.

cards.t: Ask for help before the crisis
cards.b: Emma hides her debts until the seizure order arrives, then has a single afternoon to beg Léon, Guillaumin, Binet and Rodolphe. Shame kept her silent until there were no good options left. Trouble shared early, with someone honest, can usually be managed; trouble hidden until the last day rarely can.

Emma believed happiness was always somewhere else: in Paris, in a chateau, in another man's arms. Where in your own life do you assume real happiness lies just over the horizon? What would change if you looked for something worth loving in the day you are actually living?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: One act of mercy can remake a whole life
pts.d: the Bishop's gift of the silver candlesticks turns a hardened convict into a man who spends decades doing good.

pts.h: Law without mercy becomes its own crime
pts.d: Javert hunts Valjean faithfully for twenty years, and breaks the moment he meets a goodness his rules cannot explain.

pts.h: Poverty manufactures the 'criminals' society punishes
pts.d: a loaf of bread costs Valjean nineteen years; Fantine sells her hair, her teeth, then herself to feed her child.

pts.h: Conscience is a battle fought alone, at night
pts.d: Valjean's sleepless 'tempest in a skull' over the Champmathieu trial shows that doing right costs everything you have built.

cards.b: October 1815. Napoleon has just fallen at Waterloo, the Bourbon kings are back, and France is a country of hungry poor and nervous respectable people. Into the little town of Digne trudges Jean Valjean, released from the prison galleys at Toulon after nineteen years: five for stealing a loaf of bread to feed his widowed sister's seven children, fourteen more for trying to escape. His yellow passport marks him as a dangerous ex-convict. Every inn turns him away, and even a dog kennel refuses him. He is bitter, strong as an ox, and full of hatred.

An old woman points him to the house of Monseigneur Myriel, the Bishop of Digne, a man who has given his palace to a hospital and lives on almost nothing. Myriel feeds Valjean at his table, calls him 'monsieur', and gives him a bed. In the night Valjean steals the Bishop's silver plates and flees. Gendarmes drag him back next morning. Instead of accusing him, Myriel says the silver was a gift, and asks why Valjean forgot the silver candlesticks too. Then, quietly, he tells Valjean he has bought his soul for God.

cards.q: Jean Valjean, my brother, you no longer belong to evil, but to good. It is your soul that I buy from you; I withdraw it from black thoughts and the spirit of perdition, and I give it to God.
cards.b: The Bishop's words, from Isabel Hapgood's 1887 translation, are the hinge of the whole novel. Myriel answers theft with a gift and a claim on the thief's future. Everything Valjean becomes, every risk he later takes for strangers, is an attempt to be worthy of this one undeserved act of trust.

Dazed, Valjean wanders off and, almost by reflex, steals a forty-sou coin from a small chimney-sweep, Petit Gervais. Then horror hits him; he searches for the boy in vain and weeps for the first time in nineteen years. It is his last crime. Late in 1815 a stranger reaches Montreuil-sur-Mer, finds a cheaper way to make imitation jet beads, and as Monsieur Madeleine grows rich, pays fair wages, founds schools and becomes mayor. Police inspector Javert, born in a prison, watches him. When Madeleine lifts a cart off old Fauchelevent, Javert recalls only one man that strong: a Toulon convict.

Fantine, a lovely, trusting girl from Paris, was seduced and abandoned by a rich student, Tholomyès, leaving her with a baby daughter, Cosette. Needing work, she leaves the child with innkeepers at Montfermeil, the Thénardiers, who promise care and instead treat Cosette as a servant while extorting ever-larger payments. Fantine finds work in Madeleine's factory, but a forewoman discovers her illegitimate child and dismisses her without his knowledge. To keep paying, Fantine sells her hair, then her two front teeth, then her body. Sick and broken, she blames Madeleine for everything.

One winter night a dandy, Bamatabois, shoves snow down Fantine's dress; she attacks him, and Javert arrests her, sentencing her to six months, which would kill her. Madeleine intervenes and orders her freed, overruling Javert in front of her. Fantine spits in his face; he answers by paying her debts, nursing her in his own infirmary and promising to bring Cosette to her. Humiliated, Javert denounces Madeleine to Paris as the convict Jean Valjean, only to learn that 'Valjean' has just been arrested elsewhere. Ashamed, he begs the mayor to dismiss him.

The man arrested, Champmathieu, is a confused old laborer facing life in the galleys in Valjean's place. Valjean spends a sleepless night in agony: silence keeps a town fed and lets him save Fantine; speaking frees an innocent man and sends himself back to chains. At the court in Arras he stands and declares, 'I am Jean Valjean.' He hurries back to Fantine, but Javert arrives to seize him, and she dies of shock. Returned to Toulon, Valjean in 1823 rescues a sailor from a warship's rigging, drops into the sea and is reported drowned. He has swum free.

cards.t: A doll in the dark woods
cards.b: On Christmas Eve 1823 Valjean reaches Montfermeil and finds eight-year-old Cosette alone in the night forest, hauling a bucket of water heavier than she is. He carries it for her. At the inn he sees how Madame Thénardier beats her and how the couple's daughters, Éponine and Azelma, are spoiled. He buys Cosette the magnificent doll from the toy stall she has been gazing at, then pays the scheming Thénardier fifteen hundred francs to take her away. For the first time, the child who has never been loved is held by someone who loves her.

They hide in the Gorbeau house, a shabby Paris tenement, but Javert, now in the Paris police, picks up the trail. One night he closes in with his men, and Valjean, carrying Cosette, flees through a maze of dark streets into a dead end. Using a lamp rope, he hauls them both over a high wall and lands in the garden of the Petit-Picpus convent, where the gardener is old Fauchelevent, whose life he once saved. To be admitted openly, Valjean is smuggled out in a coffin and nearly buried alive. Cosette grows up in the convent school.

Now the novel turns to Marius Pontmercy, raised by his royalist grandfather, Monsieur Gillenormand, who kept him from his father, Colonel Georges Pontmercy, a hero of Napoleon's army. After the colonel's death Marius learns how his father loved him from afar, and of his last wish: to repay a sergeant called Thénardier, who 'saved' him at Waterloo but was really robbing corpses. Marius becomes a fervent Bonapartist, quarrels with his grandfather, and lives in poverty, falling in with the Friends of the ABC, republican students led by the fierce, beautiful Enjolras.

Around 1831 Marius notices an old man and a young girl walking daily in the Luxembourg Gardens. The girl blossoms into beauty; Marius falls helplessly in love with Cosette, and Valjean, sensing danger, moves house. In his own tenement, the Gorbeau house again, Marius's neighbours are the destitute 'Jondrettes', really the Thénardiers, with Éponine, now ragged and in love with Marius. Their neglected son Gavroche lives wild on the streets. Through a hole in the wall Marius watches Thénardier and the Patron-Minette gang ambush Valjean. Javert raids; Valjean escapes.

cards.t: The garden in the Rue Plumet
cards.b: Éponine, loving Marius hopelessly, finds Cosette's address and leads him there. In the hidden garden of a house in the Rue Plumet, Marius and Cosette meet every night for weeks, innocent and ecstatic. Éponine even stops her father's gang from robbing the house. But Valjean, alarmed by warnings, decides to take Cosette to England. Marius begs his grandfather's permission to marry; Gillenormand mocks the idea and suggests he make Cosette his mistress instead. Marius storms out in despair, and returns to find the garden empty, just as Paris erupts into revolt.

At the funeral of General Lamarque, the students rise and build a barricade in the Rue de la Chanvrerie around the Corinthe wine shop. Marius joins them, wanting to die. Gavroche exposes Javert as a police spy, and he is tied up. Éponine, dressed as a boy, takes a bullet meant for Marius and dies in his arms, handing him Cosette's letter. Valjean reads Marius's farewell note to Cosette and goes to the barricade himself. Given Javert to execute, he sets him free. Gavroche is shot collecting cartridges, still singing. Enjolras falls with the rest.

As the barricade falls, Valjean lifts the unconscious Marius and drops into the sewers. He staggers for hours through the stinking dark, nearly drowning in a pit of liquid mud, only to find the outlet locked. Thénardier, hiding there, takes him for a murderer and opens the gate for a share of the 'loot', slyly tearing a strip from Marius's coat. Outside waits Javert. Valjean asks only to carry Marius home to his grandfather. Javert agrees, then lets Valjean go. Unable to live in a world where a convict is better than the law, Javert drowns himself in the Seine.

Marius recovers and marries Cosette in February 1833; Valjean gives her a fortune of nearly six hundred thousand francs. Then he confesses to Marius that he is an escaped convict. Marius, horrified, slowly freezes him out, and Valjean, deprived of Cosette, begins to die. Finally Thénardier tries to sell Marius the 'secret' that Valjean is a murderer, producing the torn coat strip as proof, and so reveals that Valjean was the man who carried Marius through the sewers. Marius and Cosette rush to him. He dies blessing them, lit by the Bishop's candlesticks.

cards.t: Jean Valjean: the saint who was a thief
cards.b: Valjean is Hugo's proof that a person is not their worst act. Brutalised by the galleys, then remade by one kindness, he spends his life repaying a debt to the Bishop by paying it forward: to Fantine, Cosette, Fauchelevent, even Javert. Yet he is never serene. Every good choice costs him something, and his hardest battles are with himself, not with the police.

cards.t: Javert: the law with a human face
cards.b: Javert is no simple villain. He is honest, incorruptible and brave, and he hounds Valjean because he truly believes order is the highest good and that criminals can never change. That belief is his whole identity. When Valjean spares his life, the system cracks: Javert cannot owe mercy to a convict, nor arrest the man who gave it. He chooses the river instead.

Where Valjean changes upward, Thénardier simply changes names: innkeeper, 'Jondrette', gang boss, blackmailer, and at last a slave trader in America. He robs the dead at Waterloo, starves Cosette and exploits his own children. Hugo shows that poverty does not automatically ennoble anyone. Yet even his daughter Éponine, raised in this greed, finds her way to a selfless death.

The novel stages a duel between two moral systems. Javert's law asks only what a man has done; the Bishop's grace asks what he might yet become. Hugo does not sneer at law, but he insists that rules applied without love become cruelty. Valjean's life is the experiment: given mercy instead of punishment, he gives back far more than any prison could extract.

cards.t: The miserable and the society that makes them
cards.b: Hugo's preface says such books are needed while ignorance and poverty exist. His 'misérables' are both wretched and, in the eyes of the law, wicked: the hungry convict, the fallen mother, the street child. Again and again he shows that the crime begins with society, in starvation wages, harsh sentences and indifference, and that charity, schooling and fair work do more than prisons.

Hugo sweeps from Waterloo to the 1832 uprising, the sewers and the convent, in long digressions that place small lives inside vast history. Yet the decisive battles happen inside one skull: Valjean deciding at Arras, Javert by the Seine, Marius choosing between love and loyalty. Revolutions may fail, Hugo suggests, but a single conscience turned toward good changes the world around it.

cards.t: Believe in someone before they deserve it
cards.b: The Bishop had every reason to call the gendarmes. Instead he handed Valjean the candlesticks too. Trust offered in advance can call out the best in a person, sometimes precisely because they know they have not earned it. Next time someone falls short, consider whether a second chance might do more than a punishment would.

cards.t: Doing right will cost you something real
cards.b: At Arras, Valjean could have kept his fortune, his good name and the town's prosperity simply by staying silent while an innocent man went to the galleys. He spoke anyway. Integrity is easy when it is free; the real test comes when it threatens what you have built. Decide in advance which lines you will not cross.

A gossiping forewoman dismissed Fantine for having a child, and a bored dandy pushed snow down her dress. Neither thought of themselves as cruel, yet together they helped destroy her. Casual judgment of people already struggling can be the push that sends them over. Notice when you are about to add weight to someone else's load.

Javert's tragedy is not that he was wicked but that he could not update. When Valjean freed him at the barricade and gave himself up at the sewer, the evidence contradicted everything Javert believed, and he had no way to bend. Hold your principles firmly, but leave room for the possibility that a person, or you, may be wrong.

Valjean's deepest fear is losing Cosette, and for a while he tries to hide her from Marius. Yet when he reads Marius's farewell letter, he walks into gunfire to save the young man who will take her away. Loving someone means wanting their happiness, even when it no longer includes you at the centre.

cards.t: Judge slowly when you know half the story
cards.b: Marius, learning that Valjean was a convict, pushed him out of Cosette's life, never imagining the old man had carried him through the sewers. Only Thénardier's clumsy blackmail revealed the truth, almost too late. When a revelation makes you want to cut someone off, ask what else about them you might not yet know.

cards.t: Kindness to children echoes for a lifetime
cards.b: A bucket carried through dark woods and an expensive doll changed Cosette's entire life, and Valjean's too. Gavroche, by contrast, ignored by his parents, still shares his bread and shelter with two lost boys. What we give the young, or deny them, shapes who they become. Look for a child near you who needs one gesture of attention.

One night of unexpected kindness from the Bishop changed the whole direction of Jean Valjean's life. Can you remember a moment when someone trusted or forgave you more than you deserved? What did it make you want to become, and is there someone in your life today to whom you could offer the candlesticks?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Flattery is cheap; honest love often sounds cold
pts.d: Goneril and Regan win kingdoms with gushing speeches, while Cordelia's plain 'Nothing' costs her everything.

pts.h: We see truly only after we lose our sight
pts.d: Lear learns wisdom only in madness, and Gloucester understands his sons only once his eyes are gone.

pts.h: Power hides what a human being really needs
pts.d: stripped of crown, knights and shelter on the heath, Lear finally pities the 'poor naked wretches' he once ignored.

pts.h: Love and forgiveness matter even when they cannot save us
pts.d: Cordelia's 'No cause, no cause' redeems Lear's last days, even though the play refuses them a happy ending.

cards.t: An old king splits his kingdom
cards.b: Ancient, pagan Britain. Lear, a king past eighty, decides to shake off the cares of state and divide his realm among his three daughters while he still lives. Goneril is married to the mild Duke of Albany, Regan to the fierce Duke of Cornwall, and the youngest, Cordelia, is courted by the King of France and the Duke of Burgundy. Lear wants to keep the title, the honours and a retinue of a hundred knights, but none of the work. And he sets a test: the daughter who says she loves him most will get the richest share.

Goneril swears she loves her father more than eyesight, space or liberty; Regan claims every other joy is dead to her beside his love. Cordelia, disgusted by the performance, says simply that she has nothing to add: she loves him as a daughter should, no more, no less. Lear explodes, 'Nothing will come of nothing', and disowns her. The loyal Earl of Kent protests and is banished on pain of death. Burgundy drops Cordelia now she has no dowry, but France marries her for her honesty and takes her away.

A second family mirrors the first. The Earl of Gloucester has two sons: Edgar, his legitimate heir, and Edmund, born out of wedlock, whom he jokes about in public. Edmund, clever and resentful, decides that 'nature' owes him what custom denies. He forges a letter in which Edgar seems to plot their father's murder, shows it to the credulous Gloucester, then warns Edgar that their father is furious. Edgar flees for his life, and Gloucester, as rash as Lear, names Edmund his true son and heir.

Lear moves in with Goneril, his hundred knights eating and brawling through her house. Within weeks she orders her steward Oswald to treat the old man coldly and demands that Lear cut his train. Two companions now speak truth to him: Kent, returned in disguise as a servant called Caius, and the Fool, whose jokes and songs keep reminding Lear that he gave away his crown and made his daughters his mothers. Stung, Lear curses Goneril with sterility and rides off, sure that Regan will treat him kindly.

Regan and Cornwall have left home to avoid him. At Gloucester's castle Lear finds his messenger, Kent, locked in the stocks for beating Oswald, an insult to the king himself. Then Goneril arrives, and the two sisters bargain him down together: fifty knights, twenty-five, ten, five, and finally, 'What need one?' Lear answers that humans are more than beasts because they need more than they need, but his voice breaks. Refusing to weep, swearing revenge he cannot name, he rushes out into a rising storm while the doors are shut behind him.

On the open heath Lear rages at the thunder, ordering the winds to crack their cheeks and flatten the world. Kent and the shivering Fool lead him to a hovel, where they find Edgar, now disguised as 'Poor Tom', a naked, babbling beggar from Bedlam. Seeing him, Lear decides this is 'the thing itself', 'unaccommodated man', and tears off his own clothes. His mind gives way. Yet in the same storm he prays, for the first time, for the 'poor naked wretches' of his kingdom he had taken too little care of.

cards.q:
I am a man
More sinned against than sinning.
cards.b: Lear says this in the storm (Act 3, Scene 2), and it is the play's turning point. It is half true: his daughters' cruelty far outweighs his folly. But the line is also self-pity, and the rest of the play pushes him past it, towards admitting his own blindness and asking Cordelia's forgiveness.

Gloucester, horrified at how the king is treated, secretly brings Lear shelter and then sends him on to Dover, where Cordelia has landed with a French army to rescue her father. Gloucester confides all this to Edmund, trusting him completely. Edmund promptly reports his father to Cornwall as a traitor in league with France, calculating that he will inherit the earldom sooner. Cornwall makes Edmund Earl of Gloucester on the spot and sends him off as escort to Goneril, who is already falling for him.

Cornwall and Regan seize Gloucester in his own house, tie him to a chair, and pluck his beard. When he admits he sent Lear to Dover, Cornwall gouges out one eye, then the other: 'Out, vile jelly!' A servant, unable to bear it, draws his sword and wounds Cornwall fatally before Regan stabs him from behind. In the dark, Gloucester calls for Edmund to avenge him. Regan tells him Edmund betrayed him. Suddenly he understands that Edgar was innocent, and she thrusts him out to 'smell his way to Dover'.

An old tenant leads the blind man onto the heath, where they meet Poor Tom. Edgar, heartbroken, keeps his disguise and agrees to guide his father to the edge of Dover cliff, where Gloucester means to kill himself, despairing that the gods kill us like flies for sport. Instead Edgar leads him to flat ground. Gloucester kneels, blesses his son, and 'jumps', falling forward a few inches. Edgar, in a new voice, tells him he has survived a miraculous fall, and Gloucester resolves to bear his suffering patiently.

The sisters' alliance rots. Albany, disgusted by Goneril's cruelty to her father, turns against her; she despises him as a milk-livered coward. Both she and the newly widowed Regan want Edmund, who has promised himself to both. Oswald, carrying Goneril's love letter, tries to kill Gloucester for the reward and is slain by Edgar, who finds a letter urging Edmund to murder Albany. Meanwhile mad Lear, crowned with weeds, meets blind Gloucester near Dover, and in fragments of wild wisdom tells him how the world rewards the rich and punishes the poor.

Cordelia's soldiers find Lear and bring him to her camp, where a doctor lets him sleep and dresses him in fresh garments. When he wakes to music, he thinks he is in hell and she is a spirit. Slowly he recognises her, kneels, and calls himself 'a very foolish fond old man', admitting she has cause to hate him. Cordelia, weeping, answers 'No cause, no cause.' It is the play's most tender moment, a reconciliation between a humbled father and the honest daughter he banished.

The British forces, led by Edmund and Albany, defeat the French army, and Lear and Cordelia are taken prisoner. Lear, astonishingly, is happy: in prison, he says, they will sing like birds in a cage, she will ask his blessing, he will ask her forgiveness, and they will outlast the great ones who ebb and flow with the moon. But Edmund, who wants no rivals to the throne he now imagines, quietly hands an officer a written order to hang Cordelia in her cell and make it look like suicide.

Albany arrests Edmund for treason. An unknown knight answers the trumpet: Edgar, who mortally wounds his brother and reveals that Gloucester died of joy and grief when he learned who his guide had been. Goneril poisons Regan and stabs herself. Dying, Edmund repents and tries to cancel his order, too late. Lear enters carrying Cordelia's body, looking for breath on her lips: 'Never, never, never, never, never.' He dies believing, perhaps, that she stirs. Kent prepares to follow his master; Edgar is left to rule a shattered land.

cards.t: Lear: a king who must learn to be a man
cards.b: Lear begins as a magnificent baby: he wants love as public applause and rages when crossed. His tragedy is that he mistakes words for feeling and titles for identity. Stripped of both on the heath, he becomes, in madness, strangely wise, pitying beggars and seeing through justice. His final kneeling before Cordelia is the only real power he ever learns.

Cordelia refuses to turn love into a speech contest, and her stubborn plainness is both her virtue and, partly, her pride. She speaks only about a hundred lines in the whole play, yet her absence shapes everything. She returns with an army not to win a crown but to rescue a father, and forgives him without a word of reproach.

Edmund is the play's most modern mind. Branded 'base' for an accident of birth, he worships raw nature instead of custom and simply takes what he wants. He is funny, frank with the audience and frighteningly efficient. Yet at the end, seeing that both sisters loved him, he wants to do 'some good', a flicker of what he might have been.

Lear and Gloucester both 'see' badly with perfectly good eyes, trusting flatterers and banishing the children who love them. Shakespeare makes the metaphor brutally literal. Only once Gloucester is blinded can he say 'I stumbled when I saw', and only in madness does Lear see the world's injustice clearly. Insight, here, is bought with loss.

The word 'nature' runs through the play. For Lear and Gloucester it means a sacred order of duty between parents and children, kings and subjects. For Edmund it means appetite and survival of the fittest. Goneril and Regan are called 'unnatural hags', yet their cruelty feels terribly human. The play asks which nature wins when order collapses.

'Nothing' echoes from Cordelia's first reply to the Fool's jokes about Lear's empty crown. The play keeps stripping people down: of land, knights, clothes, eyes, sanity. On the heath it asks what remains of a human being without possessions or rank, and answers that we are poor, bare, forked animals who need each other's care.

Lear turns affection into a competition and rewards the best performers. The result is a kingdom handed to the two people who love him least. When you ask the people close to you to prove their love in words or gestures, you train them to flatter. Watch instead for who shows up, quietly and repeatedly, when it costs them something.

cards.t: Listen to the person who annoys you
cards.b: Kent and the Fool both tell Lear the truth, one bluntly, one in riddles, and he banishes or threatens them for it. The voices that irritate us are often the only honest ones in the room. Before dismissing a critic, ask whether their worst crime is simply saying what everyone else is too careful to say.

cards.t: Don't give away power you still want to use
cards.b: Lear tries to hand over his kingdom while keeping a king's privileges, and is shocked when his daughters take him at his word. Whether you are retiring, delegating at work, or letting grown children run their own lives, be honest about what you are surrendering. Half-letting-go breeds resentment on both sides.

cards.t: Check the evidence before you condemn
cards.b: Gloucester believes a forged letter in seconds and hunts his loyal son as a murderer. He never asks to speak to Edgar, never questions the convenient informer. When a story about someone you love seems shocking, slow down and ask who benefits from your believing it. Edmund's whole career depends on people judging too quickly.

Only when he is cold and soaked on the heath does Lear think of the poor who live this way every night: 'O, I have ta'en too little care of this.' Hardship need not only embitter us. Let your own bad seasons teach you about people who live in them permanently, and let that change how you use what you have.

Edgar does not lecture his suicidal father; he walks beside him, stages a small miracle, and gives him a reason to go on. When someone you love is in despair, patience and presence often help more than arguments. 'Ripeness is all,' Edgar later tells him: endure until your time comes, not before.

cards.t: Ask forgiveness while there is time
cards.b: Lear's kneeling 'I am a very foolish fond old man' is the bravest thing he does, and it comes almost too late. Cordelia dies hours later. If there is someone you have wronged, especially someone who told you an unwelcome truth, do not wait for a perfect moment. Say sorry while the person can still hear it.

Lear could not tell the difference between people who said they loved him and the one who actually did. Think about the people in your own life: whose love is loud and whose is quiet, plain and costly? Is there a Cordelia you have overlooked or misjudged, and what could you do today to let them know you see them?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Heaven and hell are first of all states of mind
pts.d: Satan carries hell inside him wherever he flies, while Adam and Eve leave Eden promised 'a paradise within thee, happier far.'

pts.h: Freedom is real only if we are free to fail
pts.d: God makes angels and humans 'sufficient to have stood, though free to fall', and the whole poem turns on that choice.

pts.h: Wounded pride is the root of rebellion and ruin
pts.d: Satan's war begins with envy of the Son and ends with every devil hissing as a serpent in Pandemonium.

pts.h: Even after the worst failure, repair begins with humility
pts.d: Eve's plea for forgiveness breaks Adam's despair, and their tears lead to grace and a future beyond Eden.

cards.t: Fallen angels on a burning lake
cards.b: England, 1667. John Milton, blind, poor and on the losing side of a failed revolution, publishes the epic he has dictated line by line: the story of 'man's first disobedience', told so as to 'justify the ways of God to men'. Like Homer, he begins in the middle. Satan, once the brightest archangel, lies chained on a lake of fire with his rebel army after falling nine days out of Heaven. He wakes his lieutenant Beelzebub and, far from repenting, declares that it is 'better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heav'n.'

Satan heaves himself off the lake, plants his shield and spear on the burning shore, and calls his legions, who rise like autumn leaves in a stream and assemble under their banners. Milton names them as the future pagan gods: Moloch, Belial, Mammon and the rest. Though defeated, they are still magnificent, and Satan weeps before he speaks to them. Mammon's crews dig gold out of the hellish hill, and the architect Mulciber raises Pandemonium, a glittering palace where the devils, shrunk to dwarf size to fit inside, gather for a council.

In Pandemonium the devils argue about what to do next. Moloch wants open war again, whatever the cost. Belial, smooth and lazy, advises lying low in case God's anger cools. Mammon proposes building their own empire in Hell. Then Beelzebub, voicing Satan's own plan, offers a subtler revenge: God has made a new world and a new creature called Man; seduce him and they will wound God through what he loves. The assembly cheers, and Satan, playing the hero, volunteers to make the dangerous journey alone.

At the gates of Hell Satan meets two horrors. Sin, half woman and half serpent, tells him she sprang fully armed from his head when he first plotted rebellion; he lusted after her, and their son is Death, a shapeless shadow who then raped his own mother and fathered the hellhounds that gnaw her. Sin, who holds the key, opens the gates for her father. Satan launches into Chaos, a roaring abyss of warring elements, and with the help of its ruler, Chaos, struggles upward toward the light of the new world.

Milton now shifts to Heaven. God the Father watches Satan fly and tells the Son that Man will fall. He insists this is not his doing: he made angels and humans 'sufficient to have stood, though free to fall', because obedience without freedom would be worthless. Justice demands that someone pay for Man's sin, and when no angel volunteers, the Son offers to become human and die in Man's place. Meanwhile Satan disguises himself as a young cherub, fools the archangel Uriel into pointing out Eden, and lands on Earth.

On a mountain looking at Eden, Satan is torn by doubt and admits that 'myself am Hell', yet chooses evil anyway: 'Evil be thou my Good.' He leaps the wall of the garden, perches like a cormorant on the Tree of Life, and watches Adam and Eve, naked, innocent and in love. He overhears them talk of the one command God gave them: not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge. That night the angels Ithuriel and Zephon find him squatting like a toad at Eve's ear, whispering dreams. Gabriel drives him out of the garden.

Eve wakes troubled by a dream in which a voice tempted her to eat the forbidden fruit, and Adam comforts her. God sends the friendly archangel Raphael to warn Adam that an enemy is near, and that he is free and must stand firm. Eve serves the angel a meal of fruits, and Raphael, who really eats, tells the story of how the rebellion began: when God proclaimed the Son his anointed king, Satan, jealous of his rank, led a third of the angels north to revolt. Only the seraph Abdiel refused to follow him.

Raphael describes three days of war. Michael wounds Satan, who feels pain for the first time. On the second day Satan invents gunpowder and cannon and blasts the loyal angels flat; they reply by tearing up hills and hurling them on the rebels. Since angels cannot die, the fight is a stalemate, so on the third day God sends the Son alone in a fiery chariot. He drives the terrified rebels to the edge of Heaven, the crystal wall opens, and they fall nine days into Hell.

Raphael goes on to tell how the Son created the world in six days, from light to animals to Man. When Adam asks about the movements of the stars, Raphael gently tells him to be 'lowly wise' and attend to his own life. Adam then tells his own story: waking into being, naming the animals, asking God for a companion, and seeing Eve, made from his rib. He confesses that her beauty overwhelms his judgment. Raphael frowns, warns him not to let passion rule reason, and leaves.

Eight days later Satan slips back into Eden as a mist and enters a sleeping serpent. That morning Eve suggests that she and Adam garden separately to get more done. Adam worries, but she wants her virtue to be tested, and he lets her go. The serpent finds her alone, flatters her as a goddess, and claims that eating the forbidden fruit gave a mere snake speech and reason. Surely it will make her divine. Hungry, curious and convinced, Eve reaches out, plucks and eats.

cards.q: Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat / Sighing through all her Works gave signs of woe, / That all was lost.
cards.b: These lines from Book IX mark the instant Eve eats the fruit, the hinge on which the whole epic turns. Notice how quiet it is: no thunderclap, just the whole created world sighing. Milton makes the Fall feel cosmic and intimate at once, a single act of one woman in a garden wounding everything at the same time.

Elated, Eve debates whether to keep the fruit to herself so she can be Adam's equal, then, fearing she will die and he will get another Eve, decides to share it. She hurries to Adam with a branch. He is horrified, but he is not deceived: he cannot bear to live without her, so he eats knowingly, choosing her over God. At once they feel drunk with lust and make love; they wake ashamed, cover themselves with fig leaves, and spend hours in bitter mutual blame.

The Son comes to the garden to judge them: pain in childbirth for Eve, toil for Adam, death for both, and enmity between the serpent and the woman's seed. Sin and Death build a highway across Chaos to Earth. Satan returns in triumph to Pandemonium, but as the devils begin to applaud they are all turned into hissing snakes, chewing fruit that turns to ashes. On Earth, Adam despairs and turns on Eve, until she falls at his feet and begs to bear all the punishment herself. Moved, he forgives her, and together they pray.

cards.t: The world was all before them
cards.b: God accepts their prayer but they must leave Paradise. The archangel Michael comes to expel them, and first shows Adam the future from a high hill: Cain killing Abel, the Flood, the tower of Babel, Abraham, Moses, and finally Christ, who will crush the serpent and redeem humanity. Adam is amazed that so much good will come from evil. Michael promises them 'a paradise within thee, happier far.' Eve, prepared by a dream, is ready. Hand in hand, weeping a little, they walk out into the wide world.

Readers since Blake have felt Satan is the poem's most thrilling figure: brave, eloquent, defiant, 'of the Devil's party'. But watch how Milton shrinks him: from a towering archangel to a cherub, a cormorant, a toad, a snake, and finally a hissing serpent among serpents. His speeches are magnificent, and nearly every one of them is a lie, including the lies he tells himself.

Eve is no mere temptress. She is intelligent, independent and eager to prove her own virtue, which is exactly why she insists on gardening alone. Her fall comes through vanity and a real hunger for knowledge. Yet it is Eve who first breaks the cycle of blame, kneels, and offers to take all the punishment, and in that act she begins humanity's recovery.

Adam is thoughtful and articulate, a good conversationalist with angels. His weakness is that he loves Eve more than he trusts his own judgment. Raphael warns him, and still he lets her go, and then eats the fruit with his eyes open. Milton makes his sin tragically sympathetic: he falls not out of curiosity but out of loyalty and fear of loneliness.

cards.t: Free to stand, free to fall
cards.b: Milton's God insists he could have made obedient machines but did not, because love that cannot refuse is not love. Every major character, from Satan and Abdiel to Eve and Adam, faces a real choice. The poem's great wager is that a world with freedom, and therefore with the risk of disaster, is better than a safe world without it.

cards.t: The mind is its own place
cards.b: Satan boasts that 'the mind is its own place, and in it self / Can make a Heav'n of Hell, a Hell of Heav'n.' The poem proves him right in a way he hates: he carries Hell inside him even in the loveliest garden on Earth. Location matters less than the state of the soul, which is why the exiled Adam and Eve can still carry a paradise with them.

Every fall in the poem begins with someone wanting a higher place: Satan resenting the Son, Eve hoping to become a goddess, Adam refusing to be parted from his equal. Recovery runs the other way: the Son humbles himself to die, Eve kneels to Adam, and both bow in prayer. In Milton's universe, going down is the way back up.

cards.t: Name the envy behind your grievance
cards.b: Satan dresses his revolt as a fight for liberty, but it began the moment the Son was promoted over him. Before you make a principled stand, ask whether hurt pride is doing the talking. A grievance that is really envy will keep burning even after you win, just as Satan's does in the garden he has conquered.

The serpent's first move is not an argument but a compliment: it calls Eve a goddess, 'sovran of creatures'. Only after she is flattered does she listen to the reasoning. When someone praises you lavishly just before asking you to break your own rules, slow down. The compliment is often the hook, and the pitch comes next.

cards.t: Don't make big choices just to prove yourself
cards.b: Eve insists on working alone partly to show she can resist temptation unaided. Adam gives way to avoid seeming controlling. Neither choice is about the task itself; both are about how each looks. When you take a risk mainly to prove a point, you are already standing on weaker ground than you think.

cards.t: Loving someone is not the same as following them
cards.b: Adam eats the fruit because he cannot imagine losing Eve, and so he loses Paradise for both of them. Real loyalty sometimes means saying no to the person you love, or staying steady when they stumble so you can help them up. Joining someone in their mistake rarely rescues them; it only doubles the fall.

cards.t: Stop the blame spiral by going first
cards.b: After the Fall, Adam and Eve spend hours accusing each other, and Book X opens with Adam cursing Eve. The deadlock breaks only when Eve kneels and takes responsibility. In any quarrel, the person who first stops defending themselves and simply says 'I was wrong, forgive me' often turns the whole relationship around.

cards.t: Know the limits of your questions
cards.b: When Adam asks about the motions of the heavens, Raphael tells him to be 'lowly wise' and think of what concerns his own life. Curiosity is good, but some of us chase grand questions to avoid the near, practical ones. Ask what you need to know to live well today, and attend to that first.

Adam and Eve lose their perfect garden but leave with something Michael calls better: 'a paradise within'. When you lose a job, a home or a dream, you cannot go back through the gate. You can still bring your love, your faith and your character into the wide world, and build a life there.

Satan claims 'the mind is its own place', able to make a heaven of hell or a hell of heaven, yet he stays miserable in Paradise, while Adam and Eve walk out of Eden still holding hands. Where in your life are you carrying a private hell into a good place, and what would it take to carry a paradise within instead?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Civilisation is a thin coat of paint over appetite
pts.d: the Company's talk of 'progress' covers chain gangs, a grove of dying men and heads on stakes.

pts.h: Unchecked power hollows out even the most gifted person
pts.d: Kurtz arrives an eloquent idealist and ends scrawling 'Exterminate all the brutes!' beneath his own report.

pts.h: Facing the truth about yourself is a kind of victory
pts.d: Marlow honours Kurtz's dying cry, 'The horror!', as a judgment the hollow manager could never make.

pts.h: The darkness is not 'out there' but at home
pts.d: the tale begins and ends on the Thames, and the sepulchral European city is as rotten as the Congo stations.

cards.b: London, the 1890s. Five old friends sit aboard the cruising yawl Nellie, waiting for the tide at the mouth of the Thames as dusk thickens over the greatest city on earth. One of them, an unnamed narrator, muses on the river's glorious history of explorers and empire. Then the seaman Charles Marlow, sitting cross-legged like a Buddha, startles them: 'And this also has been one of the dark places of the earth.' He imagines Roman soldiers arriving in savage Britain, and begins a long, rambling story of his own.

As a boy Marlow loved the blank spaces on maps, above all one great river coiling like a snake into the heart of Africa. Years later, out of work, he gets his aunt to pull strings with a Belgian trading Company, which needs a steamboat captain because its last one, a Dane named Fresleven, was speared in a stupid quarrel over two black hens. In a city that reminds him of 'a whited sepulchre', Marlow signs papers, passes two women knitting black wool like guardians of the underworld, and lets a doctor measure his skull.

Marlow sails south on a French steamer that drops off soldiers and customs clerks along a coast of endless jungle. In one unforgettable image, a French man-of-war is shelling the bush, firing tiny shells into a continent where no enemy can be seen. Its crew, he hears, are dying of fever at the rate of three a day. The farce of it disturbs him. At the river's mouth he boards a smaller ship, and a Swedish captain tells him of a man who recently hanged himself on the road upriver.

cards.t: The Outer Station and the grove of death
cards.b: At the Company's first station Marlow finds a cliff being blasted for no purpose, machinery rusting in the grass, and a line of Africans in iron collars, chained together and called 'criminals'. In a shady grove he stumbles on starving, sick labourers who have crawled away to die, one with a bit of white worsted tied round his neck. Nearby lives the Company's chief accountant, immaculate in starched collar and white trousers, keeping perfect books. It is he who first mentions Mr Kurtz, a 'remarkable' agent who sends in more ivory than all the others combined.

cards.t: The Central Station and a sunken boat
cards.b: After a two-hundred-mile march through emptied villages, Marlow reaches the Central Station to find his steamer lying at the bottom of the river, wrecked in a suspiciously hasty trip. The station manager is a man of no talent except perfect health, who inspires only 'uneasiness'; Marlow concludes he has 'no entrails'. The agents, whom Marlow nicknames 'pilgrims', wander about with long staves, scheming for promotion. A young brickmaker who never makes bricks pumps Marlow for gossip, assuming he too is one of Kurtz's powerful sponsors in Europe.

For months Marlow tries to repair his boat, but the rivets he needs never arrive, though crates of them sit at the coast. He comes to value work itself as the one honest thing in the place, a way to 'find yourself'. Meanwhile the Eldorado Exploring Expedition, a gang of greedy adventurers led by the manager's uncle, comes and vanishes into the wilderness. Lying on the deck one night, Marlow overhears the manager and his uncle wishing Kurtz dead: he is a rival, sick and isolated, and they are happy to let the climate finish him.

cards.t: Up the river into the past
cards.b: At last the boat floats, and Marlow steams upriver with the manager, four pilgrims and a crew of African 'cannibals', who are starving yet show a restraint he finds astonishing. The voyage feels like 'travelling back to the earliest beginnings of the world'. From the banks come drumming, chanting and glimpses of dancing figures, and Marlow admits to feeling a remote kinship with that wild noise. Fifty miles below Kurtz's station he finds a hut, a stack of firewood, a note reading 'Hurry up. Approach cautiously', and a battered manual on seamanship annotated in what looks like cipher.

A thick white fog halts the boat a few miles short of the Inner Station, and from the blankness comes a terrible cry of grief. When the fog lifts, the steamer is attacked: arrows fly from the bushes, the pilgrims fire their rifles blindly into the trees, and Marlow's African helmsman, who has opened the shutter to shoot, is speared through the side. He dies at Marlow's feet, looking up with an intimate, accusing glance. Marlow blows the steam whistle and the attackers flee in terror. Then he heaves the body overboard before the hungry crew can claim it.

cards.t: The harlequin and the heads on stakes
cards.b: At the Inner Station a young Russian in a patched, motley suit, like a harlequin, greets them joyfully. He owns the seamanship book; the 'cipher' was Russian. A wanderer who has nursed Kurtz through illness, he worships him: 'This man has enlarged my mind.' Through his binoculars Marlow sees that the round knobs on the posts around Kurtz's house are human heads, all but one facing the house. Kurtz, the Russian admits, raided the country for ivory with a tribe who adored him as a god, and lacked restraint in the gratification of his lusts.

Kurtz is carried out on a stretcher, a skeletal figure seven feet long, his head like an ivory ball, his voice still deep and commanding. Hundreds of warriors pour silently from the forest, and a magnificent African woman, adorned in brass and beads, stalks to the river's edge and raises her arms toward the boat. Marlow reads Kurtz's report for the International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs: seventeen pages of soaring eloquence, ending in a scrawled postscript, 'Exterminate all the brutes!' The manager declares Kurtz's 'method' unsound, and Marlow finds himself siding with the nightmare.

That night, Marlow wakes to find Kurtz's cabin empty. He follows a trail through the wet grass and catches him crawling on all fours toward the drumming and the fires of his worshippers. Marlow faces him alone, knowing that one shout could bring the warriors down on them both. Appeals to duty or reason are useless with a man who has 'kicked himself loose of the earth'. Kurtz's soul, Marlow says, has looked into itself and gone mad. Somehow Marlow talks him back, and carries him to his bed like a child.

Next day the steamer leaves, the crowd on the bank shrieking, the woman with her arms flung up. When Marlow sounds the whistle to scatter them, the pilgrims open fire for sport. Drifting downstream, Kurtz raves about his Intended, his career and 'my ivory', and hands Marlow a packet of papers. One evening Marlow sees on his face 'sombre pride, ruthless power, craven terror' and hears him whisper his final judgment on his life. Soon the manager's servant puts his insolent head through the doorway: 'Mistah Kurtz, he dead.' The pilgrims bury him in a muddy hole.

cards.q: The horror! The horror!
cards.b: Conrad never says exactly what the horror is: the heads on the stakes, Kurtz's own soul, Europe's greed, or the human heart itself. Marlow calls it 'an affirmation, a moral victory'. Kurtz, at least, judged what he had seen, which the hollow manager, who sends a boy to announce the death, never will.

Marlow nearly dies of fever himself and returns to the sepulchral city, resenting its smug citizens. He fends off a Company man wanting Kurtz's papers, a cousin who calls Kurtz a musician, and a journalist who thinks he'd have led an extreme party. A year later he visits Kurtz's Intended, a pale woman still in mourning. She begs to hear his last words. Unable to crush her, Marlow lies: 'The last word he pronounced was your name.' On the Nellie, the tide has turned, and the Thames seems to flow 'into the heart of an immense darkness.'

A seaman of forty or so who hates a lie because it has 'a taint of death', yet ends his tale by telling one. Marlow is sceptical, ironic and humane, but no saint: he shares many prejudices of his age, and he chooses Kurtz's nightmare over the manager's. Conrad lets him circle and stumble, because the truth he is trying to tell keeps slipping away.

cards.t: Kurtz: the voice without a centre
cards.b: Painter, musician, poet, journalist, 'an emissary of pity and science', Kurtz is Europe's best self sent into Africa. 'All Europe contributed to the making of Kurtz.' Alone with absolute power and no police, neighbours or public opinion, he becomes a god demanding heads on stakes. Marlow keeps calling him 'a voice': brilliant words with nothing solid behind them, 'hollow at the core'.

Kurtz is monstrous on a grand scale; the manager is monstrous in a smaller, more frightening way. He has no ideas, no vision, no gifts except never falling ill, and he runs the station by inspiring uneasiness. He objects to Kurtz not because Kurtz is cruel but because his 'method' is bad for business. He is the system that survives every Kurtz.

Conrad had captained a Congo steamer in 1890, at the height of King Leopold's plunder, and he saw the gap between 'civilising' rhetoric and reality. The book's Company calls itself a bringer of light while working men to death for ivory. 'The conquest of the earth', Marlow says, 'is not a pretty thing when you look into it too much.'

The title points three ways: the African interior, the corruption of Europe, and the darkness in every human heart. Marlow's frame on the Thames insists that London too was once a 'dark place', and the tale ends there. Restraint, not race or rank, is the only thing that separates people from savagery, and the starving cannibals show more of it than the pilgrims.

cards.t: Can the truth be told at all?
cards.b: The novella is about the difficulty of telling it. Marlow's meaning, the narrator warns, is not inside the tale like a kernel but around it like a haze. Fog blinds the boat, notes are mistaken for cipher, and the story ends with a lie. In 1975 Chinua Achebe argued the book itself silences Africans, denying them speech and history, and that critique is now part of reading it.

cards.t: Watch the gap between mission and method
cards.b: The Company prints noble words and runs chain gangs; Kurtz writes a moving report and scrawls 'Exterminate all the brutes!' beneath it. When an organisation or a person speaks beautifully about its aims, look at what it actually does to the people with the least power. The postscript, not the speech, is the truth.

cards.t: Build guard rails before you need them
cards.b: Kurtz falls because nothing outside him says no: no neighbours, no law, no friend willing to contradict him, only a worshipful Russian. Marlow says such men lack 'restraint'. Whatever power you hold, at work, at home or online, keep people around you who are free to tell you you're wrong, and listen when they do.

Surrounded by intrigue at the Central Station, Marlow holds on by fixing his wrecked boat, rivet by rivet. 'I like what is in the work, the chance to find yourself.' When an environment is absurd or corrupt, a concrete, honest task you can do well is an anchor that keeps your judgment clear.

cards.t: Beware of being dazzled by eloquence
cards.b: The Russian harlequin gives up his judgment to Kurtz because Kurtz talks so magnificently: 'This man has enlarged my mind.' Even Marlow is half-seduced by 'the voice'. Charisma is not character. Admire a speaker's gifts if you like, but judge them by the heads on the stakes, not the poetry.

The accountant keeps perfect books a few yards from men dying in a grove; the manager shrugs at murder because it's 'unsound method'. Neither lifts a weapon, yet both keep the machine running. Ask what your neat columns and routine tasks are part of, and whether you would approve of the whole if you saw it.

cards.t: Judge yourself before life is over
cards.b: Marlow honours Kurtz for one thing: at the end he looked squarely at what he had become and pronounced a verdict. 'The horror!' is terrible, but it is honest. You need not wait for a deathbed. A regular, unflinching look at your own conduct is the first step to changing it.

cards.t: Some truths need care in the telling
cards.b: Marlow, who hates lies, cannot bring himself to tell the grieving Intended the truth, and readers still argue whether his lie is mercy or cowardice. Honesty matters, but so does knowing what a truth will do to the person hearing it. Before you deliver a hard fact, ask whether you are serving them or yourself.

Kurtz went into the jungle full of noble ideas and became a monster once nobody was watching and nobody could say no. Marlow believes what saves most of us is not virtue but a policeman round the corner and a neighbour's opinion. If no one could ever see or check what you do, which of your principles would still hold, and which ones are really just habits of being watched?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: You cannot outsource your conscience
pts.d: Dorian hands his sins to a painting, yet every cruelty still lands on him, and finally kills him.

pts.h: Clever words can corrupt as surely as deeds
pts.d: Lord Henry never commits a crime; his witty paradoxes and a yellow book do the damage instead.

pts.h: Beauty without a moral life becomes a mask
pts.d: Dorian's flawless face hides a soul the attic portrait shows as cunning, bloodstained and loathsome.

pts.h: A double life is a prison, not a freedom
pts.d: eighteen years of hiding the locked schoolroom leave Dorian fearful, isolated and driven to murder.

cards.t: A painter's secret in a summer studio
cards.b: London, the 1880s, high society at its most elegant and idle. In a studio full of the scent of roses and lilac, the painter Basil Hallward puts the last touches to a full-length portrait of an astonishingly beautiful young man. His friend Lord Henry Wotton, a languid aristocrat famous for his epigrams, calls it Basil's masterpiece. Basil refuses to exhibit it: he has put 'too much of myself' into it. The sitter, Dorian Gray, has become his whole inspiration, and he begs Henry not to meet him, fearing his influence.

Dorian arrives anyway, and Lord Henry goes to work. While Basil paints, Henry speaks of a 'new Hedonism': youth is the only thing worth having, every impulse we strangle poisons us, and 'the only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it.' Dorian, twenty and innocent, feels as if a hidden chord has been struck. Out in the garden, Henry warns him that his beauty will fade within a few years and leave him hideous and spent. For the first time, Dorian is frightened of time.

cards.t: The wish that sells a soul
cards.b: When Basil unveils the finished picture, Dorian sees his own loveliness as if for the first time, and then sees what Henry has taught him to see: that the canvas will stay young while he withers. In anguish he wishes it were the other way round, and that he would give his soul for it. Basil, hurt that his friend now loves the picture more than him, reaches for a palette knife to destroy it. Dorian stops him: 'It would be murder!' The portrait is sent to his house.

cards.t: The bargain, in his own words
cards.q: If it were only the other way! If it were I who was to be always young, and the picture that was to grow old! For that—for that—I would give everything! Yes, there is nothing in the whole world I would not give! I would give my soul for that!
cards.b: Dorian says this half in tears, standing before Basil's finished canvas. No devil appears, no contract is signed; Wilde's Faust story turns on a passing outburst of vanity. That is the chilling part. The novel suggests that we sell our souls not in grand pacts but in moments of self-pity, and only discover later that someone was listening.

Lord Henry, curious, learns Dorian's history from his uncle: a beautiful mother, Lady Margaret Devereux, whose penniless husband was killed in a duel arranged by her own father. Weeks later Dorian confesses he is in love. In a shabby little theatre in the East End he has found Sibyl Vane, a seventeen-year-old actress who plays Juliet, Rosalind and Imogen with such genius that he worships her. He calls her art incarnate. She knows nothing of him but calls him 'Prince Charming'. Dazzled, he announces their engagement.

In the Vanes' cramped lodgings, Sibyl glows with happiness, while her mother, a faded actress, thinks mostly of the money a gentleman might bring. Her brother James, a rough, loving sailor about to ship out for Australia, is suspicious of this rich stranger whose name Sibyl does not even know. Walking with her in the park, he catches sight of the man but loses him in the crowd. Before he leaves, James swears that if 'Prince Charming' ever does his sister wrong, he will hunt him down and kill him.

Dorian brings Lord Henry and Basil to see Sibyl play Juliet. She is dreadful: wooden, artificial, mechanical. The audience jeers. Backstage she explains joyfully that real love has shown her that the stage was only shadows; she can no longer pretend to feel what she now truly feels. Dorian, who loved her only as an artist, is disgusted. 'You have killed my love,' he tells her coldly, and leaves her sobbing on the floor. He wanders London until dawn, then returns home to his library.

In the grey morning light Dorian glances at the portrait and freezes: there is a new touch of cruelty about the painted mouth. The wish has come true. Shaken, he resolves to be good, to marry Sibyl, and writes her a passionate letter of apology. Then Lord Henry arrives with news: Sibyl was found dead in her dressing room, having swallowed poison.
