Henry recasts her death as a beautiful tragedy, a Jacobean heroine's ending. Within hours Dorian is dressing to join him at the opera.

cards.t: The locked room and the yellow book
cards.b: Basil comes to comfort Dorian and is shocked by his calm. When the painter asks to see the portrait, Dorian flies into a rage; Basil confesses he once idolised him and feared the picture revealed it. Dorian has the canvas carried to the dusty old schoolroom at the top of the house, draped in a purple satin pall, and keeps the only key. Lord Henry sends him a strange French novel bound in yellow, the life of a man who pursues every sensation. It becomes Dorian's bible.

Years pass. Dorian studies perfumes, music, jewels, embroideries and the sins of history, while his face stays boyish and pure. Rumours gather: he is seen in low dens by the docks; friends he touches are ruined. A young Guards officer kills himself; Adrian Singleton is disgraced; Lord Kent's son and the Duke of Perth's circle sink in scandal. Society shudders yet still invites him. Night after night he climbs to the locked room, compares his smooth face with the ageing, coarsening portrait, and gloats.

cards.t: Basil sees the soul, and dies
cards.b: On the eve of Dorian's thirty-eighth birthday, Basil calls on his way to Paris to beg him to answer the rumours. 'I shall show you my soul,' Dorian says, and leads him upstairs. Basil recognises his own brushwork in a leering, withered face, and begs his friend to pray. Seized by sudden hatred, Dorian stabs him with a knife. Next day he blackmails Alan Campbell, a chemist and former friend, with an unnamed secret, forcing him to destroy the body. Campbell later shoots himself.

cards.t: Prince Charming in the opium den
cards.b: Haunted, Dorian drives to an opium den near the river, where he meets the wrecked Adrian Singleton. As he leaves, a ravaged woman sneers at him as 'Prince Charming'. A sailor lunges out of the dark: James Vane, home at last, who has hunted that name for eighteen years. Dorian saves himself by pointing to his face: how could a man of twenty have known Sibyl? James lets him go, only for the woman to laugh that Dorian has not changed in eighteen years.

At his country house, Selby Royal, Dorian sparkles among guests, trading wit with the Duchess of Monmouth, until he sees James Vane's white face pressed against the conservatory glass and faints. For days he dares not leave the house. Then, on a shooting party, his guest Sir Geoffrey Clouston fires at a hare and kills a man hidden in the thicket. Dorian goes to the stable to look at the body: it is James Vane. Weeping with relief, he believes himself safe at last.

cards.t: The knife turned on the picture
cards.b: Back in London, Dorian tells Lord Henry he means to reform: he has spared a village girl, Hetty Merton, whom he could have ruined. Henry laughs, insisting Dorian could never commit a crime. Upstairs, Dorian hopes the portrait has improved, but sees only a new look of cunning, the smirk of the hypocrite, and fresher blood on the hand. Even his goodness was vanity. In fury he seizes the knife that killed Basil and plunges it into the canvas, meaning to kill its evidence.

A horrible cry wakes the house. Servants break in through the roof and find, on the wall, a splendid portrait of their master in all his wonderful youth and beauty, exactly as Basil painted him. On the floor lies a dead man in evening dress with a knife in his heart, withered, wrinkled and loathsome of visage. Only by the rings on his hands do they recognise who he is. Wilde's ending is swift and merciless: in destroying the picture, Dorian has destroyed himself.

cards.t: Dorian Gray: the beautiful blank page
cards.b: Dorian begins almost without a self, a lovely surface onto which Basil projects adoration and Lord Henry projects theory. His tragedy is that he becomes what others tell him he is. He is capable of remorse, which makes him more than a monster, but every good impulse is swallowed by fear and vanity. He wants consequences without change, and the portrait lets him pretend he can have it.

Henry is the funniest voice in the novel and its most dangerous. He tosses off paradoxes ('the only thing worse than being talked about is not being talked about') and never acts on any of them. His wife leaves him; he barely notices. He treats Dorian as a fascinating experiment, then refuses to believe the experiment could end in murder. Words, for him, have no weight. The novel proves him wrong.

cards.t: Basil Hallward: the painter as conscience
cards.b: Basil is shy, earnest and decent, and he loves Dorian with an artist's devotion he half fears to confess. He is the only person who tells Dorian the truth to his face, urging him to pray even after seeing the hideous picture. That honesty gets him killed. Wilde once said Basil was what he thought he was himself: the man who pours his soul into art and pays for it.

cards.t: Art for art's sake, on trial
cards.b: Wilde's preface declares 'There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book' and 'All art is quite useless.' Then he writes a novel that punishes a man for living as though life were only art. Dorian treats Sibyl as a performance and his own existence as a collection of sensations. The book stages the aesthete's creed and shows its cost, without ever giving up its love of beauty.

cards.t: The hidden self and the public mask
cards.b: Victorian London prized respectability above almost everything, and the novel is full of men leading double lives: Dorian's smooth face over his rotting portrait, rumours whispered behind drawing-room doors. Wilde, who lived a hidden life of his own, knew the strain of it. The locked schoolroom is every secret we keep from others, and the portrait is the truth that keeps recording, whether anyone sees it or not.

cards.t: Influence: how ideas get into us
cards.b: 'All influence is immoral,' Lord Henry says, while influencing Dorian completely. The novel is fascinated by how a voice, a book or a picture can rearrange a person from the inside. Henry's talk, the poisonous yellow novel, even Basil's adoring painting each shape who Dorian becomes. Yet Wilde does not let Dorian off: he chose which voices to follow, and which to stab.

Dorian's face never changes, but the portrait does, line by line: a cruel mouth after Sibyl, blood after Basil. Real life has no magic canvas, yet our habits, relationships and reputations quietly record what we do. Behaving well only when consequences are visible is a bet you will eventually lose. Act as if there were a portrait upstairs keeping score.

cards.t: Love the person, not the performance
cards.b: Dorian adores Sibyl as Juliet and drops her the moment she becomes simply herself, a girl in love. Many of us fall for an image: a partner's charm, a friend's status, a colleague's polish. Ask whether you would still care if the performance faltered on a bad night. Sibyl died of that question; you can at least ask it in time.

Lord Henry is wonderful company, and he never lifts a finger, yet his clever sayings send Dorian down every dark road. Be careful whose voice becomes the one in your head. Someone who makes every scruple sound naive and every indulgence sound sophisticated is not freeing you. Ask what their ideas have done for their own lives; Henry's wife left him.

cards.t: Hiding a mistake makes it grow
cards.b: Dorian could have confessed his cruelty to Sibyl, or shown Basil the picture honestly. Instead he locks the room, and secrecy breeds more secrecy: one hidden sin requires a murder, the murder requires blackmail, the blackmail requires a suicide. In ordinary life too, the cover-up usually costs more than the original fault. Tell the truth early, while it is still small.

cards.t: Goodness done for show doesn't count
cards.b: Dorian spares Hetty Merton and expects the portrait to reward him, but it shows only the new smirk of the hypocrite. He was being good in order to feel good about himself. Real change is not a transaction with your reputation. If you do something kind, do it because it is right, not because you are hoping someone, even your own conscience, will applaud.

cards.t: Don't let fear of ageing run your life
cards.b: The whole catastrophe begins when Lord Henry frightens a twenty-year-old about losing his looks. Dorian trades his soul to stay young and ends up unable to grow at all: no wisdom, no deepening love, no real friends. Ageing is the price of experience. Spend less energy holding on to who you were and more on becoming someone worth growing old as.

cards.t: Listen to the friend who tells the truth
cards.b: Basil is the only one who confronts Dorian about the rumours and begs him to change, and Dorian kills him for it. That is the extreme version of something common: we resent the people who see us clearly and drift toward those who flatter. Notice who in your life is willing to make you uncomfortable out of love, and keep them close.

Dorian keeps a locked room where the truth about him is stored, and spends his life making sure nobody climbs the stairs. Most of us have a smaller version: a habit, a resentment, a way we treat someone when no one is watching. If your own portrait were hanging upstairs this morning, what would it show, and what one thing could you do today to change it?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Society judges women by a cruel double standard
pts.d: Angel confesses his own past and is forgiven; Tess confesses hers, an assault, and is abandoned.

pts.h: Purity lives in intention, not in history
pts.d: the novel's defiant subtitle, 'A Pure Woman', insists that what was done to Tess does not define her.

pts.h: Chance and timing can wreck a life
pts.d: a letter slipped under a carpet and a husband back days too late decide Tess's fate.

pts.h: Rigid ideals can be crueller than open vice
pts.d: Angel's high-minded principles wound Tess more deeply than Alec's frank selfishness ever could.

cards.t: A haggler learns he is a knight
cards.b: Wessex, Hardy's half-imagined south-west England, in the 1870s or 1880s, when old village life is giving way to railways and machines. In the village of Marlott, in the green Vale of Blackmoor, a shiftless, hard-drinking carrier named John Durbeyfield is told by a passing parson that he descends from the d'Urbervilles, a great Norman family now extinct. The news goes straight to his head. His eldest daughter, Tess, sixteen, beautiful and serious, is dancing with the other girls at the May-Day club-walk. A gentleman's son, Angel Clare, joins the dance, but chooses another partner.

That night John is too drunk to drive the beehives to Casterbridge market, so Tess sets out before dawn with her little brother Abraham. Tired, she falls asleep at the reins; the morning mail-cart runs into them in the dark lane, and its shaft pierces the old horse, Prince, who bleeds to death in the road. The family's living dies with him. Tess blames herself completely. So when her mother, Joan, proposes that she go and 'claim kin' with a rich Mrs d'Urberville near Trantridge, guilt overrides her pride and she agrees.

The Trantridge 'd'Urbervilles' are no relations at all: a merchant named Simon Stoke made his fortune in the north and simply bought the old name. His son, Alec, a swaggering young man with a moustache and a cigar, meets Tess, feeds her strawberries from his own fingers and pins roses to her breast. He arranges a job for her tending his blind mother's poultry. For weeks he pursues her, driving her at reckless speed down hills to force her to cling to him, demanding kisses. Tess resists, but she needs the wages for her family.

One September Saturday, Tess walks home from the market town of Chaseborough with a group of tipsy farm workers. A quarrel breaks out with Car Darch, one of Alec's cast-off favourites, who wants to fight her. Alec rides up and offers escape; Tess leaps onto his horse. He deliberately loses the way in The Chase, an ancient wood, wraps her in his coat as she sleeps in the fog, and there, in the dark, he violates her. Hardy leaves the act half-veiled, but leaves no doubt about who is guilty and who innocent.

Tess stays at Trantridge a few weeks, then walks home in October, refusing Alec's money. On the road a man paints Bible texts on stiles: THY, DAMNATION, SLUMBERETH, NOT. Months later she gives birth to a son. She works in the harvest fields, nursing him at noon while the village whispers. When the baby falls ill, her father, ashamed, bars the parson from the house, so Tess baptises the child herself by candlelight, naming him Sorrow. He dies. The vicar will not give a full Christian burial; Sorrow lies in the churchyard's neglected corner.

cards.t: The Valley of the Great Dairies
cards.b: Two and a half years pass. At twenty, Tess resolves to begin again where nobody knows her, and takes work as a milkmaid at Talbothays, a rich dairy farm in the lush valley of the River Froom run by the genial Dairyman Crick. In this fertile, slow-moving place she revives like a plant. Among the workers is Angel Clare, the young man from the May dance, youngest son of an evangelical vicar. Angel has refused to enter the Church and is learning farming so he can run a farm abroad or at home.

Angel notices Tess when she speaks of how souls can leave the body by gazing at a star. Through a summer of dawns in the mist and evenings among the cows, they fall deeply in love. The other milkmaids, Izz Huett, Marian and Retty Priddle, love Angel too, hopelessly, and know he wants Tess. In a famous scene, after a summer flood, Angel carries all four girls in turn across a drowned lane. Tess is moved by her rivals' generosity and feels she has no right to take him from them.

Angel proposes. Tess refuses again and again, haunted by her past, yet cannot help loving him. Her mother writes telling her never to reveal it: 'Many a woman have had a Trouble.' Finally, on the eve of the wedding, Tess writes Angel a full confession and pushes it under his door. It slides beneath the carpet. He never sees it. On the wedding morning she finds it still lying there, unread, and tears it up. They marry at New Year, and an afternoon cock crows at them as they leave, an omen everyone notices.

cards.t: Two confessions on the wedding night
cards.b: They spend their wedding night in an old farmhouse at Wellbridge that once belonged to the d'Urbervilles; portraits of sinister d'Urberville women stare from the walls. By the fire, Angel confesses that in London he once spent forty-eight hours of 'dissipation' with a stranger. Tess, relieved, gladly forgives him, and tells her own story, certain he will forgive her in turn. He does not. Stunned, he says the woman he loved was not her but 'another woman in your shape'. Her pleading changes nothing.

cards.t: The words that end a marriage
cards.q: O Tess, forgiveness does not apply to the case! You were one person; now you are another.
cards.b: Angel speaks these words on the wedding night, minutes after Tess has freely forgiven his own confession. Notice the cruelty hiding in his logic: he does not deny she is the same woman he loved an hour ago; he simply decides she cannot be. An idea in his head has replaced the person in front of him. The whole second half of the novel unfolds from this sentence.

For a few cold days they live as strangers. One night Angel sleepwalks, carries Tess across a swollen river and lays her tenderly in an empty stone coffin in a ruined abbey, murmuring 'my wife, dead, dead!' Then he leaves for Brazil to try farming there, telling her not to come to him. Before going he impulsively asks Izz Huett to come with him as his mistress; Izz admits that nobody could love him more than Tess did, and, ashamed, he drops her off at home. Tess gives most of her allowance to her parents.

By winter Tess is a field labourer at Flintcomb-Ash, a bleak, stony upland farm, hacking frozen swedes in sleet beside her old friend Marian under a vindictive farmer, Groby. She snips off her eyebrows to make herself plain. Desperate, she walks fifteen miles to Emminster to ask Angel's parents for help, but she overhears his priggish brothers sneering about Angel's marriage, and finds one of them has picked up the boots she hid in a hedge. Her courage fails, and she turns back without ever knocking at the vicarage door.

On the way home she hears a barn preacher: it is Alec, now a Methodist convert, won over, ironically, by Angel's father. Seeing Tess unsettles his new faith at once. He follows her to Flintcomb, makes her swear on an ancient stone, Cross-in-Hand, never to tempt him, then abandons preaching altogether and pursues her as before. During the brutal threshing at the farm, driven by a steam machine, he pesters her until she strikes him across the mouth with her heavy leather glove and draws blood. 'Once victim, always victim,' she cries.

Tess's father dies; the family's lease on the cottage ends, and on Lady Day they are evicted. Homeless, they camp beside the d'Urberville tombs in Kingsbere church. Alec offers to house and support her mother and the younger children, and Tess, her letters to Angel unanswered, finally yields. Meanwhile Angel, wasted by fever in Brazil and humbled by a stranger's wiser view of her, comes home and searches for her. He finds her at the fashionable resort of Sandbourne, in a lodging house, dressed in fine clothes. 'It is too late,' she tells him.

When Angel leaves, Tess stabs Alec through the heart; the landlady sees the blood spreading on the ceiling. Tess runs after Angel and tells him what she has done, and at last he forgives her completely. For a few days they hide in an empty mansion in the New Forest, happy. Fleeing north, they reach Stonehenge at night; Tess lies down on an altar stone and sleeps. At dawn police surround them. 'I am ready,' she says. She is hanged at Wintoncester while Angel and her sister 'Liza-Lu watch the black flag rise.

cards.t: Tess: the pure woman Hardy defends
cards.b: Tess is proud, sensitive and fiercely loyal, carrying her family's needs on her back from the night Prince dies. Hardy's subtitle, 'A Pure Woman', was a provocation in 1891: he insists that her inner purity survives what men and chance do to her. Her tragedy is partly her own goodness: her honesty, her self-blame, her willingness to sacrifice herself for others.

Alec d'Urberville is the stage villain in a modern suit: moustache, cigar, gig driven too fast. Yet Hardy makes him oddly consistent. He wants Tess and says so; his conversion collapses the moment he sees her. He exploits her family's poverty with cold intelligence, buying her as his father bought a name. His power is money, and he knows exactly how to use it.

cards.t: Angel: the gentle man who fails
cards.b: Angel Clare is a freethinker who has rejected his father's church, and yet he is the harshest judge in the book. He loves an ideal, 'a fresh and virginal daughter of Nature', not the real woman. His tragedy is that his liberalism stops exactly where his own pride begins. Brazil and suffering teach him mercy, but only after his rejection has destroyed the woman he loved.

The wedding night is the novel's moral centre: two confessions, one forgiven, one not. Angel's lapse was chosen; Tess's was forced on her, yet she alone is punished. Hardy indicts a whole Victorian code that measured a woman's worth by her sexual history while excusing men. Contemporary reviewers were scandalised, which was exactly the point.

cards.t: Fate, chance and the indifferent gods
cards.b: Hardy's universe is not malicious so much as careless. A dozing girl kills a horse; a letter slides under a carpet; a husband returns days too late. At the end Hardy writes that 'the President of the Immortals' had 'ended his sport with Tess'. The bitterness is aimed at a world where small accidents of timing decide whole lives.

In the fields and dairies Tess is in harmony with the natural world, and Hardy suggests that nature condemns nothing; only society calls her 'fallen'. Meanwhile the old rural order is breaking down: the threshing machine drives the workers, families are evicted, and the d'Urberville name itself is bought and sold. Tess is crushed between ancient bloodline and modern market.

cards.t: Judge the act, not the label
cards.b: Angel cannot see Tess the moment she becomes 'a woman with a past'. A category replaces the person he married. When you learn something hard about someone you love, ask what they actually did, what was done to them and who they are today, before any label does the thinking for you.

cards.t: Hold yourself to your own rule
cards.b: Angel asks forgiveness and receives it in seconds, then refuses the same mercy minutes later. Hypocrisy rarely feels like hypocrisy from the inside; it feels like having standards. Whenever you are about to condemn someone, check honestly whether you have already excused yourself for something similar.

cards.t: Say the hard thing face to face
cards.b: Tess's confession goes under a carpet, and her life turns on that small failure of delivery. A note slipped under a door lets us feel we have spoken while leaving the outcome to luck. If something truly matters, make sure the other person has actually heard it, and hear their answer.

cards.t: Guilt is not the same as responsibility
cards.b: Tess treats Prince's death, a sleepy accident caused by her father's drinking, as a crime that she must pay for, and that guilt sends her to Trantridge. Taking responsibility is healthy; carrying blame that belongs to others can lead you straight into danger. Ask honestly whose fault something really was.

Again and again Tess's 'decisions' are made for her by need: the horse, the eviction, the hungry children camped by a tomb. Alec's power is economic before it is anything else. Before judging someone's choices, ask what their real alternatives were; and where you can, help widen them.

cards.t: Mercy delayed can be mercy denied
cards.b: Angel does learn to forgive, fully and sincerely, in Brazil. But by the time he arrives at Sandbourne, Tess has already been forced back to Alec. Forgiveness has a season. If you know you will one day forgive someone, consider doing it while it can still change the story.

cards.t: Begin again where you can grow
cards.b: After Sorrow's death, Tess does not stay in Marlott under the village's eyes; she walks to Talbothays and blossoms. Changing your surroundings is not running away when the old place keeps you defined by your worst moment. Sometimes healing needs new soil, new work and people who meet you fresh.

Angel's failure was not a lack of love but a failure to let the real Tess replace the picture of her he carried in his head. Most of us carry pictures like that, of a partner, a child, a friend or ourselves. Whose real self might you be refusing to see today, and what would change if you saw them as they are?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: A conscience can be trained to do wrong
pts.d: Huck believes helping Jim escape is a sin, yet his heart keeps overruling the morality his society taught him.

pts.h: Real friendship ignores the lines society draws
pts.d: on the raft Huck and Jim become equals, and Jim proves the most loyal and generous person in the book.

pts.h: Civilization is often a polite mask for cruelty
pts.d: feuds, lynch mobs, swindles and slave sales flourish among the 'respectable' people of every riverside town.

pts.h: Freedom is found in honesty, not escape alone
pts.d: the river frees Huck and Jim only while they are truthful with each other; on shore, lies and cons take over.

cards.t: A boy who won't be civilized
cards.b: The Mississippi valley in the 1830s or 1840s, when Missouri is a slave state and the great river is the highway of a raw young nation. In the town of St. Petersburg, Huckleberry Finn, a ragged boy of about thirteen, tells his own story in his own rough voice. After the adventures of Tom Sawyer, Huck has six thousand dollars in gold held in trust by Judge Thatcher, and the kindly Widow Douglas and her stern sister, Miss Watson, are trying to 'sivilize' him with shoes, schooling and prayers. He finds it all suffocating.

cards.t: Pap comes back for the money
cards.b: Huck's father, Pap, a violent drunk whom everyone thought dead, reappears and demands the boy's fortune. Judge Thatcher protects the money, so Pap kidnaps Huck and locks him in a lonely log cabin on the Illinois shore. At first Huck rather enjoys the idleness, but the beatings worsen, and one night Pap, raving with delirium tremens, chases him with a knife, calling him the Angel of Death. Huck plans his escape carefully: he saws through the wall, kills a wild pig, smears its blood about, and fakes his own murder.

Huck paddles a canoe to Jackson's Island, in the middle of the river, and hides there while the town fires cannon over the water to raise his 'drowned' body. On the island he stumbles on Jim, Miss Watson's enslaved man, who has fled because he overheard her planning to sell him down the river to New Orleans for eight hundred dollars, away from his wife and children. Huck, taught that helping a runaway is a crime and a disgrace, nonetheless promises not to tell. A storm-tossed house floats past with a dead man inside; Jim covers the face.

Restless, Huck disguises himself as a girl and slips into a riverside town for news. A sharp woman, Mrs Judith Loftus, sees through his disguise when he threads a needle and throws a lump of lead like a boy, but she tells him something more important: many suspect Jim of murdering Huck, there is a three-hundred-dollar reward, and her husband is heading to the island that very night. Huck races back and wakes Jim with the words 'They're after us!' They load a raft and push off downriver in the dark.

cards.t: Life and lies on the raft
cards.b: The plan is to float to Cairo, Illinois, then steam up the Ohio River into the free states. They travel by night and hide by day, and on the raft Huck feels 'free and easy and comfortable'. They board a wrecked steamboat, the Walter Scott, and narrowly escape a gang of murderous robbers. Then a thick fog separates them. When Huck finds Jim again, he pretends the whole night was a dream. Jim, who had grieved for him, rebukes him for the cruel joke, and Huck, ashamed, apologizes to him.

As they near Cairo, Huck's conscience torments him: by his society's rules he is stealing poor Miss Watson's 'property'. He sets off in the canoe resolving to turn Jim in. But Jim calls him the only white gentleman who ever kept his promise to him, and when two men hunting runaways come alongside, Huck lies, hinting that his family on the raft has smallpox. Frightened, they float him money and leave. Then they see the clear Ohio water mixing with the muddy Mississippi: they have drifted past Cairo, deeper into slave country.

One night a steamboat smashes through the raft and Huck and Jim are separated. Huck swims ashore and is taken in by the Grangerfords, a gracious, wealthy Kentucky family with fine furniture, sentimental poetry by a dead daughter, Emmeline, and Sunday sermons on brotherly love. They are also locked in a decades-old blood feud with the Shepherdsons, though nobody remembers why it began. When young Sophia Grangerford elopes with Harney Shepherdson, the feud erupts into slaughter, and Huck's friend Buck is shot dead. Sickened, Huck flees to the river, where Jim has quietly mended the raft.

Two ragged con men beg a place on the raft. The younger claims to be the rightful Duke of Bridgewater; the older trumps him by claiming to be the lost Dauphin, heir to the throne of France. Huck sees at once they are frauds but humours them to keep the peace. They take over the raft and fleece town after town: the King poses as a repentant pirate at a camp meeting, and they stage a shameful show called the 'Royal Nonesuch'. In Bricksville, Huck watches Colonel Sherburn shoot a harmless drunk and scornfully face down a lynch mob.

Hearing that a tanner named Peter Wilks has died, the King and Duke pose as his brothers from England, Harvey and William, to claim his fortune, including six thousand dollars in gold. They weep theatrically over the coffin, fool the townspeople, and sell the family's enslaved people, splitting mothers from children. Huck, moved by the kindness of Peter's niece Mary Jane, steals the gold and hides it in the coffin. When the real brothers arrive, the town digs up the grave to settle the matter; the gold is found, and in the uproar Huck and the con men all escape.

cards.t: Jim is sold for forty dollars
cards.b: Downriver in Arkansas, the King betrays Jim, selling him for forty dollars to a farmer named Silas Phelps as a runaway with a reward on his head. Huck faces the crisis of his life. Everything he has been taught says that God will damn him for helping a slave escape. He writes a letter to Miss Watson telling her where Jim is, and for a moment feels cleansed. Then he remembers Jim on the raft: singing, standing his watches for him, calling him the best friend he ever had. He trembles, and tears up the letter.

cards.t: The most famous decision in American fiction
cards.q: All right, then, I'll go to hell.
cards.b: Huck says this as he tears up the letter that would return Jim to slavery. He truly believes he is choosing damnation. Twain's irony is that the boy's 'wickedness' is the noblest act in the book, while the respectable religion that condemns him upholds slavery.

cards.t: Tom Sawyer arrives at the Phelps farm
cards.b: Huck walks to the Phelps farm, determined to steal Jim out of slavery. By pure chance, Aunt Sally Phelps mistakes him for her nephew, Tom Sawyer, who is expected for a visit, and Huck plays along. When the real Tom arrives, he gleefully takes the name of his brother, Sid. To Huck's amazement, Tom, a 'respectable' boy, agrees to help free a slave. Meanwhile the townsfolk catch the King and Duke, and Huck watches the two frauds ridden out of town, tarred and feathered. Despite everything, he feels sorry for them.

Jim is locked in a simple hut and could be freed in minutes, but Tom insists on an escape worthy of his adventure books. He makes them dig with case-knives, bakes a rope ladder into a pie, has Jim scratch mournful inscriptions and a coat of arms, write a journal in blood and keep rats, spiders and snakes as prison companions. Jim endures it all patiently. Tom even sends anonymous letters warning the Phelpses of a gang of cutthroats, because a proper escape needs danger. Weeks pass in this foolish, cruel game.

The night of the escape, armed farmers are waiting, and Tom is shot in the leg. Jim refuses to leave the wounded boy and helps the doctor nurse him, giving up his own freedom; he is recaptured and chained. Then Tom, recovering, reveals the truth: Miss Watson died two months ago, ashamed of planning to sell Jim, and freed him in her will. Tom knew all along and staged the whole adventure for fun. Aunt Polly arrives and identities are untangled. Jim reveals that the dead man in the floating house was Pap. Huck's money is safe.

Jim, free at last, is given forty dollars by Tom for being such a patient prisoner, and recalls with pride that he once predicted he would be rich. Tom wears the bullet from his leg on a watch-guard around his neck. Aunt Sally now proposes to adopt Huck and civilize him, and Huck has had enough of that. He closes his story by saying he means to 'light out for the Territory ahead of the rest', westward into the wild, because he has been civilized before and cannot stand it.

cards.t: Huck Finn: the outcast with a sound heart
cards.b: Huck is uneducated, superstitious and a fluent liar, the son of the town drunk. Yet he sees the world with a clear, unsentimental eye, and his instinctive sympathy keeps defeating the prejudices he has absorbed. Twain described him as a boy with a sound heart and a deformed conscience. His voice, colloquial and funny, changed American writing for ever.

cards.t: Jim: the book's true moral centre
cards.b: Jim is a husband and father fleeing to keep his family together, and he dreams of buying them out of slavery. Superstitious and sometimes played for comedy, he is also wise, tender and selfless: he stands Huck's watches, mourns him in the fog and gives up his freedom to save Tom. He is the only adult in the book who acts like a real father to Huck.

Tom is clever, charming and full of borrowed ideas from adventure novels. Huck admires him, but the last chapters expose him: he toys with a man's freedom for his own amusement, knowing Jim is already free. Tom stands for the 'respectable' boy whose games are harmless only to himself, and for a South intoxicated by romantic fantasies of honour and chivalry.

Huck's conscience is not his inner voice of goodness: it is the voice of his society, which teaches that slavery is right and that helping Jim is theft. His heart, shaped by friendship, tells him otherwise. The novel's great drama is a boy learning to trust his own feeling over what church, law and town insist is moral.

The raft is a small world where Huck and Jim live simply, share food and stories and treat each other as equals. The shore is where greed, violence and hypocrisy wait: feuds, mobs, frauds and slave catchers. Yet the river is not an escape, because the shore keeps invading the raft, and the current carries Jim ever deeper south.

Twain fills the riverbanks with pious, polite and respectable people who own human beings, feud to the death, lynch and swindle. The Grangerfords go to church with their guns; Aunt Sally, told a steamboat explosion killed only an enslaved man, answers that it is lucky 'nobody' was hurt. Twain's satire asks what such a civilization is worth, and why a runaway boy sees more clearly than it does.

cards.t: Question what you were taught is right
cards.b: Huck sincerely believes that helping Jim is a sin, because every adult he knows says so. His decision to tear up the letter shows that inherited morality can be badly wrong. When a rule demands that you betray a person in front of you, examine the rule, not just your guilt.

cards.t: Apologize, even when it costs your pride
cards.b: After the fog trick, Huck sees how much he has hurt Jim and makes himself go and apologize, though his society says a white boy owes no apology to an enslaved man. He says he was never sorry for it afterwards. Swallowing pride to repair a friendship is almost always worth it.

cards.t: Know people by what they do
cards.b: The King and Duke wear grand titles; the Grangerfords have fine manners; Jim is called property. Their actions tell the truth: the 'nobles' are thieves, the gentlefolk kill children, and Jim gives up his freedom to save a wounded boy. Judge people by their deeds, not by their status or their labels.

cards.t: Don't follow the crowd into cruelty
cards.b: Colonel Sherburn scorns the Bricksville lynch mob as cowards who are brave only in numbers, and they slink away. The Wilks townsfolk are fooled by tears and showmanship. Twain repeatedly shows crowds being stupid, gullible and violent. Notice when you are being swept along, and ask whether you would act this way alone.

cards.t: Other people's lives are not your game
cards.b: Tom's elaborate 'evasion' turns Jim's suffering into his own entertainment, and someone gets shot for it. It is a sharp warning about treating real people's struggles as material for our stories, causes or amusement. When you help someone, ask what they actually need, not what makes you feel heroic.

Huck cannot overturn slavery or reform the river towns, but he can hide the Wilks gold for Mary Jane, lie to the slave hunters and refuse to send the letter. He even pities the tarred and feathered frauds. A life of decency is built from such small, concrete choices, made one at a time.

cards.t: Loyalty is proved in hard moments
cards.b: Jim could have run when Tom was shot, and nobody would have blamed him. Instead he stays, helps the doctor and is chained again for it. Huck, too, risks everything for Jim at the Phelps farm. Friendship is not what we say on easy days but what we do when it costs us.

Huck's 'conscience' was really the voice of his town, and following his heart felt like sin. Every age has its accepted wrongs that decent people defend without thinking. Is there something you were taught is simply right that you have never really examined? What would it take for you to tear up that letter?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Feeling needs judgment to be safe
pts.d: Marianne's open, unguarded love for Willoughby nearly destroys her; it is passion without sense that wounds.

pts.h: Restraint is not the absence of feeling
pts.d: Elinor suffers as deeply as her sister over Edward but carries it silently, out of duty to others.

pts.h: Money quietly decides who may love whom
pts.d: Willoughby, Lucy Steele and Mrs Ferrars all bend hearts to fortunes; few marriages here escape the ledger.

pts.h: Steady worth outlasts glamour
pts.d: the dull-seeming Colonel Brandon and shy Edward prove truer than the charming Willoughby ever was.

cards.b: England in the 1790s, when a gentleman's estate passed to his son and daughters could be left with almost nothing. Henry Dashwood dies at Norland Park in Sussex, and the house goes to John, his son by a first marriage. John promises his dying father to help his stepmother and half-sisters, Elinor, Marianne and young Margaret. Then his grasping wife Fanny talks him down, step by comic step, from three thousand pounds to the occasional present of game. The four women are left with five hundred pounds a year.

cards.t: Sense and sensibility, side by side
cards.b: The two elder sisters give the book its title. Elinor, nineteen, has feelings as strong as anyone's but governs them; she keeps the family's accounts, its manners and its nerve. Marianne, sixteen, is all sensibility: she adores Romantic poetry, dead leaves and wild hills, despises caution, and believes true love strikes only once. Their mother is as impulsive as Marianne. At Norland, Elinor grows quietly attached to Fanny's brother, Edward Ferrars, a shy, kind young man who wants only a quiet life as a clergyman.

Fanny makes it cuttingly clear that Edward is meant for a rich bride, so Mrs Dashwood accepts a cottage in Devonshire from a cousin, Sir John Middleton. At Barton Park they meet his cold, elegant wife; her mother, Mrs Jennings, a vulgar, warm-hearted widow devoted to matchmaking; and Colonel Brandon, a grave bachelor of thirty-five. Brandon falls silently in love with Marianne, who finds him ancient and dull, a man who wears flannel waistcoats. Edward's farewell was strangely reserved, and Elinor cannot tell what he feels.

cards.t: A hero appears in the rain
cards.b: Running down a hill in a sudden storm, Marianne falls and twists her ankle. A handsome stranger, John Willoughby, sweeps her up and carries her home. He is staying with a rich elderly relative, Mrs Smith, whose estate he expects to inherit. He loves the same poets and music as Marianne, and within days they are inseparable. He offers her a horse, cuts a lock of her hair, and takes her alone round the house he will one day own. Everyone assumes an engagement; nobody has actually announced one.

Colonel Brandon receives a letter and abruptly cancels a pleasure outing, riding off to London without explanation. Soon after, Willoughby too leaves in haste, claiming Mrs Smith has sent him on business, and gives no promise of return. Marianne weeps theatrically and refuses to eat or sleep, thinking misery a proof of love. Then Edward visits Barton, low-spirited and evasive, wearing a ring with a plait of hair he says is his sister's. Elinor suspects it is her own, and is puzzled by his gloom.

Two vulgar young cousins of Mrs Jennings arrive: silly Anne Steele and her sharp, flattering sister Lucy. Lucy singles out Elinor and, swearing her to secrecy, confides that she has been secretly engaged to Edward Ferrars for four years, since he was a boy at her uncle's school. She produces his portrait and a letter as proof. The ring's hair was Lucy's. Elinor understands that Lucy suspects her and is warning her off. She keeps the secret, hides her pain and pities Edward, trapped by a youthful promise.

In January, Mrs Jennings takes the sisters to London. Marianne writes eagerly to Willoughby; he does not answer. At a crowded evening party she sees him and rushes forward; he greets her coldly and turns away. Next morning comes his letter, perfectly polite and utterly heartless: he regrets any misunderstanding, returns her letters and the lock of hair, and announces his engagement to Miss Grey, an heiress worth fifty thousand pounds. Marianne collapses in grief, and only now admits they were never engaged at all.

cards.q: The more I know of the world, the more am I convinced that I shall never see a man whom I can really love. I require so much!
cards.b: Marianne says this early in the novel, at sixteen, sure that only a soul exactly like her own will do. Willoughby seemed to be that soul. Now, holding his cold letter, she learns what her demand for perfect sympathy cost her: she judged him by his taste in poetry, not his character. The line is funny at first; by this point it hurts.

Colonel Brandon tells Elinor what he knows. As a youth he loved his cousin Eliza, who was forced to marry his elder brother for her fortune; she fell into disgrace and died poor. Brandon took charge of her little daughter, also Eliza. The letter that called him away revealed that young Eliza had been seduced, made pregnant and abandoned by Willoughby. Brandon later fought him in a duel. Hearing this, Marianne is shocked, but her grief only deepens; she loses colour, appetite and hope.

Anne Steele blurts out Lucy's engagement to Fanny, who throws Lucy out of her house in hysterics. Mrs Ferrars demands that Edward break it off; he honourably refuses to desert Lucy, so his mother disinherits him and settles his fortune on his foppish brother Robert. Marianne learns Elinor has known for four months, suffering silently while comforting her. Ashamed, Marianne sees her sister anew. Then Colonel Brandon, pitying Edward, offers him a small church living at Delaford, and asks Elinor, of all people, to deliver the offer.

Travelling home, the sisters stop at Cleveland, the Somerset house of Mrs Jennings's daughter Charlotte Palmer and her sneering husband. Marianne, still careless of herself, takes long walks in wet grass at dusk, catches a putrid fever, and comes close to death. Elinor nurses her through the night while Colonel Brandon rides to fetch their mother. Just as the fever breaks, a carriage arrives. It is not Brandon but Willoughby, who has driven all the way from London on hearing Marianne is dying.

Half drunk and desperate, Willoughby tells Elinor everything. He first courted Marianne idly, then truly loved her, and meant to propose. But Mrs Smith learned of young Eliza and demanded he marry the girl; he refused, was disinherited, and, deep in debt, chose the heiress instead. His new wife, jealous, dictated that brutal letter. He is miserable and wants Marianne to think a little less badly of him. Elinor, against her judgment, feels pity: he is weak and selfish, not a monster, and he has punished himself.

Marianne recovers slowly at Barton, chastened. She sees that her own neglect of herself nearly killed her and grieved everyone who loved her, and she resolves to live by reason, study and kindness. When Elinor tells her Willoughby's story, she decides she could never have been happy with a man who chose money over honour. Then the servant Thomas brings news from town: Mr Ferrars is married to Miss Lucy Steele. Elinor's composure finally breaks, and her mother realises how much she has hidden.

Edward himself arrives, awkward and anxious. It was Robert, the new heir, whom Lucy married; she simply switched to the richer brother. Edward is free, and within the hour he proposes to Elinor, who bursts into tears of joy. Mrs Ferrars grudgingly allows him some money, and the couple settle at Delaford parsonage. Over time, Marianne comes to love Colonel Brandon and marries him at nineteen. Willoughby lives on, comfortably enough, regretting what he lost. Lucy, endlessly flattering, worms her way into Mrs Ferrars's favour.

Elinor is the novel's moral centre and its most private sufferer. She loses Edward, keeps Lucy's secret, manages her mother's money and nurses her sister, all while hiding a broken heart. Austen does not make her cold: her joyful tears at the end show what restraint has cost. Elinor's 'sense' is not caution for its own sake but consideration, a refusal to make others pay for her pain.

cards.t: Marianne Dashwood: the heart on fire
cards.b: Marianne is generous, gifted, honest and maddening. She will not tell polite lies, scorns gossip and dullness, and gives herself completely. Austen loves her and criticises her: her contempt for convention is partly vanity, and her worship of feeling makes her blind to Willoughby and unkind to Brandon and Mrs Jennings. Her illness and recovery turn her from a reader of romances into a wiser woman.

Austen sets two suitors side by side. Willoughby is everything romance promises: handsome, eloquent, passionate about art, and fatally weak where money is concerned. Brandon is everything romance overlooks: older, quiet, scarred by an old sorrow, and steadily, practically good. He rescues the wronged, helps Edward and fetches a mother to a sickbed. The novel quietly asks which kind of man truly loves.

The title sounds like a contest, but Austen wants a blend. Sensibility, the cult of fine feeling fashionable in the 1790s, makes Marianne vivid and brave but self-absorbed. Sense makes Elinor wise but nearly silent about her own heart. By the end Marianne learns judgment and Elinor finally lets her feelings show. Each sister needed a little of the other.

cards.t: Money, marriage and women's precarious lives
cards.b: The first chapter is about inheritance, and the shadow of money never lifts. The Dashwood women cannot earn or inherit much; marriage is their only path to security. Men, too, are shaped by fortunes: Willoughby sells himself, Edward is punished for keeping his word, Robert is rewarded for nothing. Austen exposes, with wit and anger, a world where love is constantly priced.

Nearly every crisis turns on concealment: Edward's engagement, Brandon's history, Willoughby's seduction, Elinor's grief. Polite society demands masks, and characters like Lucy and Fanny exploit them, saying sweet things while acting cruelly. Elinor keeps secrets out of honour; Lucy keeps them as weapons. The novel asks when silence is integrity and when it is merely a strategy.

cards.t: Don't mistake shared taste for character
cards.b: Marianne falls for Willoughby because he loves the same poems and music. That tells her nothing about whether he keeps promises or pays his debts. When choosing a partner, friend or colleague, notice what people do when it costs them something, the way Brandon quietly helps Edward, not what they enthuse about at a dinner party.

cards.t: Keep your word even when it hurts
cards.b: Edward made a foolish promise to Lucy as a lonely teenager, yet he refuses to break it, even when his mother strips him of his fortune. His integrity costs him everything and then, unexpectedly, wins him everything. Being trustworthy is not a calculation about rewards; but over time people notice who stands by their commitments.

Marianne starves herself and walks in the rain, believing suffering proves love. It nearly kills her and terrifies her family. Elinor grieves just as truly while still eating, working and caring for others. Let yourself feel loss fully, but don't make your pain into a show or a punishment; the people around you have to live with it too.

Marianne dismisses Colonel Brandon as old and boring because he wears flannel and speaks little. Behind that surface are a tragic past, deep loyalty and real generosity. The quiet person in the corner may be the most interesting one in the room. Ask a question before you write someone off.

cards.t: Promises made to the dying are still promises
cards.b: John Dashwood swears to provide for his sisters, then lets Fanny argue him down to nothing in a single comic conversation. Good intentions shrink fast once self-interest starts negotiating. If you mean to be generous, act quickly and decide the amount before the reasons for giving less start sounding reasonable.

Lucy Steele praises Lady Middleton's spoilt children, confides in Elinor to warn her off, and finally charms Mrs Ferrars into favour. Her sweetness is always aimed at an advantage. When someone's warmth seems oddly targeted, ask what they want; and when you praise others, make sure you mean it.

cards.t: Judge people with mercy as well as truth
cards.b: Elinor despises what Willoughby has done but still hears his confession and feels pity. She doesn't excuse him; she understands him. Holding someone accountable and recognising their humanity are not opposites. It is possible to say: this was wrong, and the person who did it is more than the wrong.

Elinor and Marianne each have half of what a wise life needs. Elinor guards her heart so carefully that almost no one knows it is breaking; Marianne shows hers so freely that it is trampled. Which sister are you more like? Is there a feeling you are hiding that someone you trust should know, or one you are displaying that would be better held with a little more sense?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Society manufactures the criminals it fears
pts.d: the workhouse starves Oliver and the slums hand him to Fagin; Dickens blames the system before the boy.

pts.h: Goodness can survive a terrible upbringing
pts.d: Oliver stays honest through every corruption the book throws at him, and Nancy finds courage amid squalor.

pts.h: Charity without compassion is cruelty
pts.d: Mr Bumble and the board feed paupers gruel and sermons, while Brownlow and the Maylies offer real kindness.

pts.h: Violence and fear destroy those who live by them
pts.d: Sikes murders Nancy and is hunted to his death; Fagin ends trembling in the condemned cell.

cards.b: England in the 1830s, just after the New Poor Law of 1834 herded the destitute into workhouses run on deliberately harsh rules so that poverty would be punished rather than relieved. In one such workhouse a young woman, found collapsed in the street, gives birth to a boy and dies. No one knows her name. The parish beadle, the pompous Mr Bumble, invents a surname for the orphan from his alphabetical list: Twist. Oliver spends his first nine years in a baby farm run by Mrs Mann, who pockets most of the money meant to feed him.

At nine Oliver returns to the workhouse proper, where the boys are fed three thin bowls of gruel a day and slowly starve. Driven by hunger, they draw lots to decide who will ask for a second helping, and the lot falls to Oliver. He walks up to the master, bowl in hand, and makes his famous request. The officials are scandalised; the board of gentlemen declare the boy will be hanged one day, lock him in a dark room, and post a notice offering five pounds to anyone who will take him away.

cards.t: The most famous request in English fiction
cards.q: "Please, sir, I want some more."
cards.b: Five small words from a starving nine-year-old holding out an empty bowl, and the whole system shudders. Dickens makes the officials' horror the joke and the indictment at once: in a world organised to keep the poor 'in their place', asking for enough to live on is treated as rebellion. It is the moment Oliver stops being a parcel passed between institutions and becomes a person.

Oliver narrowly escapes being bound to a brutal chimney sweep and is instead apprenticed to Mr Sowerberry, the undertaker, who finds the boy's sad, pale face perfect for walking ahead of children's funerals. He sleeps among the coffins and eats the dog's scraps. Noah Claypole, an older charity-boy apprentice, bullies him relentlessly, and one day insults Oliver's dead mother. Oliver, normally meek, flies at him and thrashes him. Beaten and shut in the cellar for it, he slips out at dawn and walks seventy miles toward London, the only place large enough to hide in.

Footsore and starving on the road at Barnet, Oliver meets Jack Dawkins, the Artful Dodger: a swaggering boy in a man's coat who buys him a meal and promises free lodging with a 'respectable old gentleman' in London. The gentleman is Fagin, a shrivelled old receiver of stolen goods who keeps a den of child pickpockets in the slums near Saffron Hill. Fagin welcomes Oliver warmly, feeds him sausages, and teaches him a 'game' of lifting handkerchiefs from his pockets. Oliver, innocent to the point of comedy, has no idea he is being trained as a thief.

cards.t: Caught, and rescued by Mr Brownlow
cards.b: Sent out at last with the Dodger and Charley Bates, Oliver watches in horror as they pick the pocket of an elderly gentleman browsing at a bookstall. He runs; the crowd cries 'Stop thief!' and Oliver, not the real thieves, is knocked down and dragged before Mr Fang, a bullying magistrate. The bookseller arrives to clear him just as Oliver faints. The victim, the kindly Mr Brownlow, takes the feverish boy home to Pentonville, where his housekeeper Mrs Bedwin nurses him. Brownlow is struck by Oliver's likeness to a portrait of a young woman hanging on his wall.

Fagin fears Oliver will betray the gang. His partner Bill Sikes, a violent housebreaker with a savage dog named Bull's-eye, sends his lover Nancy to find the boy. When Brownlow, to prove a sceptical friend wrong, trusts Oliver to return some books and five pounds to the bookseller, Nancy and Sikes seize him in the street, Nancy loudly posing as his heartbroken sister. Back in the den Fagin strips him of his new clothes. Brownlow, finding the boy gone and hearing Bumble's lying account of a vicious orphan, sadly concludes Oliver was a thief after all.

Fagin wants Oliver criminally compromised so he can never go back. Sikes needs a small boy to crawl through a window, so he takes Oliver on a night journey up the Thames valley to burgle a house at Chertsey with his accomplice Toby Crackit. Oliver resolves to wake the household the moment he is inside, but the servants hear the noise first and fire. Oliver is shot in the arm. Sikes carries him a little way, then dumps him in a ditch and flees as the pursuit closes in. Wounded and feverish, Oliver crawls back to the very house.

The house belongs to Mrs Maylie, a gentle elderly lady, and her adopted niece Rose, a girl of seventeen with an orphan's history of her own. Instead of handing the wounded boy to the police, they listen to his story, and their cheerful friend Dr Losberne bullies the servants into muddling their evidence so he cannot be identified. Oliver recovers and spends a blissful summer with them in the countryside. Rose falls dangerously ill and recovers; Mrs Maylie's son Harry proposes to her, but Rose refuses him, fearing her obscure birth will ruin his political career.

Meanwhile a sinister stranger called Monks, a pale, scarred man prone to fits, is paying Fagin to make Oliver a convicted criminal. Monks traces Oliver's origins back to the workhouse, where Bumble has married the matron, Mrs Corney, for her furniture and found himself henpecked. Old Sally, a pauper nurse, had robbed Oliver's dying mother of a gold locket and confessed it on her deathbed to Mrs Corney. The Bumbles sell the locket and a ring, engraved 'Agnes', to Monks, who drops them through a trapdoor into the rushing river so no proof survives.

Nancy overhears Monks telling Fagin his plan: he is Oliver's half-brother, and he means to rob the boy of his inheritance and see him hanged. Drugging Sikes with laudanum, she slips away to a West End hotel and, ashamed of her own ragged appearance, tells everything to Rose Maylie. Rose begs her to leave her life of crime, but Nancy refuses; she will not abandon Sikes, whom she loves. Rose seeks advice from Mr Brownlow, whom Oliver has just joyfully found again, and the two arrange to meet Nancy secretly on London Bridge.

Suspicious of Nancy, Fagin sets Noah Claypole, who has come to London and joined the gang, to follow her. On the steps of London Bridge at midnight Noah overhears Nancy describing Monks to Brownlow and Rose, while still refusing to betray Fagin or Sikes. Fagin twists the report to make Sikes believe she has informed on him. Before dawn Sikes goes home and beats Nancy to death with his pistol and a club as she clutches Rose's handkerchief and prays for mercy. It is the most savage scene Dickens ever wrote.

Sikes flees into the countryside but cannot escape Nancy's staring eyes, which haunt him everywhere. He tries to drown his dog, which knows too much, but it escapes him. Returning to London, he hides in a ruined house on Jacob's Island, a stinking slum by the Thames, but the dog leads a furious mob there. Sikes climbs onto the roof with a rope, meaning to lower himself into the ditch below. Seeing Nancy's eyes again, he stumbles; the noose slips around his neck and he hangs himself. The dog leaps after him and dies.

Brownlow seizes Monks, whose real name is Edward Leeford, and forces a confession. His father, Edwin Leeford, trapped in a bitter marriage, loved Agnes Fleming and left her and their unborn child a fortune; Monks's mother destroyed the will. Agnes was the woman in Brownlow's portrait, and Rose is her younger sister, which makes Rose Oliver's aunt. Fagin is arrested, tried and sentenced to hang; Oliver visits him in the condemned cell and finds him raving. The Bumbles lose their posts and end as paupers in the workhouse they once ruled.

Freed from the stain of uncertain birth, Rose marries Harry Maylie, who gives up his ambitions to become a village clergyman. Mr Brownlow adopts Oliver and moves with him to live near them, so the boy at last has a family and an education. Oliver generously shares his inheritance with Monks, who squanders it, sinks back into crime and dies in prison in America. Charley Bates, shocked by Sikes's crime, turns honest and becomes a cheerful farmer; the Dodger is transported to Australia. In the village church, a white marble tablet bears one word: Agnes.

cards.t: Oliver: innocence that will not bend
cards.b: Oliver is less a realistic child than a test case. Dickens asks whether goodness can survive the workhouse, the undertaker's cellar and Fagin's den, and answers yes. Oliver is passive, often fainting or fevered, and critics find him bland, but his stubborn purity is the point: every adult who meets him reveals their own nature by how they treat him. His rare flashes of spirit, like thrashing Noah, show the dignity beneath the meekness.

Fagin is one of Dickens's great grotesques: witty, affectionate, playful with his boys, and utterly ruthless, happy to see them hanged if it keeps him safe. He is also a troubling creation, repeatedly labelled 'the Jew' in a way that drew on ugly stereotypes; Dickens, challenged by a Jewish reader, cut most of those references in later editions. His final night in the condemned cell is a terrifying study of a mind collapsing under fear.

cards.t: Nancy: a thief with a conscience
cards.b: Nancy is the novel's most complex soul. Raised in Fagin's world, she helps recapture Oliver, then is horrified by what she has done and risks her life to save him. Yet she will not leave Sikes, who beats her, because she loves him and believes she is too far gone for any other life. Her courage and her trap are equally real, and her murder is the moral centre of the book.

cards.t: Poverty is a policy, not a sin
cards.b: Dickens wrote Oliver Twist partly as an attack on the New Poor Law, which assumed the poor were idle and must be made miserable to discourage dependency. His savage irony, 'the board were very sage, deep, philosophical men', exposes officials who starve children while feasting themselves. The novel insists that the workhouse and the slum are man-made, and that they breed exactly the crime respectable society then hangs.

Why does Oliver stay good when everything around him should corrupt him? Dickens half-answers with blood: Oliver is a gentleman's son, and goodness seems to run in his veins. But he also shows nurture at work: the Dodger and Charley were never given a chance, and Nancy's tragedy is that she glimpses goodness too late. The book never fully reconciles the two explanations, and that tension still provokes readers.

The novel moves between the sunlit, orderly world of Pentonville and Chertsey and the dark, filthy maze of Saffron Hill and Jacob's Island. Respectable people barely know the slums exist; Rose and Nancy meeting on London Bridge is a rare crossing between them. Dickens drags his middle-class readers down the alleys, making them smell and see what their comfort is built on.

Oliver's request for more gruel takes enormous courage and brings him punishment, yet it is the first act that sets his story moving. Sometimes asking for what is fair will be treated as insolence by those who benefit from silence. Ask anyway, plainly and politely. The discomfort of the people you ask is not proof that you were wrong to ask.

cards.t: Judge systems by how they treat the weakest
cards.b: The parish board call themselves charitable while children starve under their care. Mr Fang dispenses 'justice' by bullying a fainting boy. Dickens invites us to test every institution, a school, a company, a government office, by asking how it treats the person with the least power in the room. Fine words in the rulebook matter less than gruel in the bowl.

cards.t: Kindness to a stranger can change a life
cards.b: Mr Brownlow could have pressed charges against the boy accused of robbing him; instead he took Oliver home, nursed him, and believed him. The Maylies did the same with a wounded burglar's accomplice. Neither had any reason to expect a reward. Small, specific acts of trust toward someone others have written off are often the turning point of that person's life.

cards.t: Beware the warmest welcome from the wrong people
cards.b: Fagin and the Dodger are the first people ever to be friendly to Oliver: a hot meal, a bed, jokes and games. That warmth is the bait. When someone in need is offered easy belonging, ask what is being asked in return. Exploiters rarely look cruel at first; they look like the only people who care.

cards.t: Loving someone does not oblige you to stay
cards.b: Nancy saves Oliver but will not save herself, choosing to return to Sikes because she loves him and feels she owes him loyalty. That choice costs her her life. Her story is a hard reminder that love and danger can coexist, and that leaving a violent relationship is an act of self-respect, not betrayal. Accepting help when it is offered can be the bravest choice.

Sikes escapes the police for days, but not Nancy's eyes. Every field, every room, every shadow brings her back to him, until his own terror makes him slip on the roof. Whatever we think of punishment, Dickens shows how a wrong done lives on in the one who did it. Facing a wrong early is easier than fleeing it forever.

Mr Bumble is a tyrant to paupers and a coward to his wife; his cocked hat and gold-laced coat are his whole identity. When he loses his post he loses himself. Watch how people use small authority, a uniform, a title, a key to the storeroom. It tells you more about them than anything they say, and it is worth asking the same question of yourself.

Oliver meets two kinds of adults: those who see a pauper, a thief, a problem to be disposed of, and those like Brownlow and Rose who see a frightened child worth saving. Think of someone in your life, or someone you pass every day, whom it would be easy to write off. What might change if you looked at them the way Mr Brownlow looked at Oliver?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: A story always reveals its teller
pts.d: the Miller, Reeve, Wife of Bath and Pardoner each expose themselves more vividly in their tales than in their portraits.

pts.h: Experience can talk back to authority
pts.d: the Wife of Bath sets five marriages against centuries of learned books, and makes the books look thin.

pts.h: Hypocrisy flourishes inside respectable institutions
pts.d: the Pardoner, Friar, Summoner and Monk sell holiness for profit, while the poor Parson simply lives it.

pts.h: Laughter and faith belong to the same journey
pts.d: bawdy tales, saints' lives and a closing sermon ride side by side on one road to Canterbury.

cards.t: April on the road to Canterbury
cards.b: England in the late 1380s: a country still reeling from the Black Death, shaken by the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, where the old order of knights, clergy and labourers is giving way to merchants, lawyers and self-made widows. One April evening, when spring makes people long to go on pilgrimage, the narrator, a mild and observant man called Chaucer, stops at the Tabard Inn in Southwark, south of London. There he meets twenty-nine travellers heading for the shrine of the martyr Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral, and he joins them.

The General Prologue sketches each pilgrim, and together they make a cross-section of society. There is the noble Knight, home from crusades, and his fashionable son the Squire; the dainty Prioress, Madame Eglentyne, who weeps over mice and speaks French with an English accent; a hunting Monk; a smooth-talking Friar; a solemn Merchant secretly in debt; a poor Oxford Clerk who would rather buy books than clothes; the gap-toothed, much-married Wife of Bath; the saintly Parson and his brother the Plowman; a brawny Miller; a sour Reeve; a pimpled Summoner; and the Pardoner with his bag of fake relics.

The innkeeper, a loud and genial man named Harry Bailly, decides to ride along and run the company. He proposes a contest: each pilgrim will tell two tales on the way to Canterbury and two on the way home, and whoever tells the story of 'best sentence and moost solaas', the most meaning and the most delight, will win a free supper at the Tabard paid for by everyone else. Harry will be judge. Everyone agrees. Next morning they set out, draw straws to decide who goes first, and the lot falls, conveniently and properly, to the Knight.

cards.t: The Knight's tale of rival cousins
cards.b: The Knight tells a long, stately romance set in ancient Athens. Two Theban cousins, Palamon and Arcite, sworn brothers captured in war, both fall in love with Emelye, the sister-in-law of Duke Theseus, after glimpsing her from their prison tower. Their love turns their brotherhood into bitter rivalry. Theseus finally stages a grand tournament: Arcite prays to Mars for victory, Palamon to Venus for Emelye. Both prayers are granted. Arcite wins, but a fall from his horse kills him, and after years of mourning Palamon marries Emelye. Theseus closes with a speech about accepting fate with grace.

cards.t: The drunken Miller breaks the order
cards.b: The Host politely invites the Monk to follow, but the Miller, drunk and pale, bellows that he has a tale to match the Knight's, and will not wait. So rank collapses into comedy. His tale tells of John, an old Oxford carpenter, his lively young wife Alisoun, and their lodger, the clever student Nicholas, who convinces John that a second Flood is coming so he can spend the night with Alisoun. A lovesick parish clerk, Absolon, begs a kiss at the window, receives a very rude one, and returns with a red-hot plough blade. The roof comes down laughing.

The Reeve, an old carpenter himself, takes the Miller's tale as a personal insult and replies with one about a cheating miller. Symkyn, a proud miller near Cambridge, steals grain from two students, John and Aleyn, who revenge themselves by sleeping with his wife and daughter in a farcical night of mistaken beds. This is how the whole book works: tales become weapons, and pilgrims 'quite', or pay back, one another. The Cook starts a tale of a London apprentice that breaks off unfinished, and the Man of Law tells of Custance, a patient Christian princess cast adrift at sea.

cards.t: The Wife of Bath speaks for herself
cards.b: Then comes Alisoun, the Wife of Bath, with a prologue longer than many tales. 'Experience', she announces, is authority enough for her. She has had five husbands since she was twelve, and she argues with Scripture and the Church Fathers about virginity, marriage and desire. Three husbands were rich and old, and she ruled them. Her fifth, the young clerk Jankyn, read to her nightly from a book of wicked wives. She tore pages out; he struck her so hard she went partly deaf. In the end he burned the book and gave her mastery, and they lived happily.

Her tale is an Arthurian romance with a sting. A knight of Arthur's court rapes a young woman and is condemned to death, but Queen Guinevere gives him a year and a day to discover what women most desire. Everyone gives a different answer. At last a hideous old woman offers him the true one, if he will grant whatever she asks. Before the queen he answers: sovereignty. He is saved, and the old woman demands marriage. In bed she asks him to choose between her ugly and faithful or beautiful and free. He lets her choose, and she becomes both beautiful and true.

cards.t: The answer that saves the knight
cards.q: Wommen desiren to have sovereynetee / As wel over hir housbond as hir love.
cards.b: This is the answer the knight gives Queen Guinevere in the Wife of Bath's Tale: women want rule over their husbands as well as their lovers. It is the turning point of the whole collection, opening a lively argument about marriage and power that the Clerk, the Merchant and the Franklin will each answer in turn.

cards.t: Feuds, fiends and a famous fart
cards.b: The Friar and the Summoner, professional rivals who both live off sinners, now trade insults through stories. The Friar tells of a greedy summoner who befriends a yeoman in green, who turns out to be a devil; when an old widow sincerely curses the summoner, the devil happily carries him off to hell. The furious Summoner replies with a tale of a begging friar who pesters a sick man named Thomas for a gift. Thomas hands him a fart, and the tale ends with a squire working out how to divide it equally among twelve friars.

Others take up the question of marriage. The Clerk tells of patient Griselda, a peasant girl married to the marquis Walter, who tests her by taking away her children and pretending to divorce her; she never complains, and is finally restored. The bitter Merchant tells of old January, who marries young May and is tricked in a pear tree under his very eyes. The Franklin offers a gentler ideal: Dorigen and Arveragus marry as equals, and when a rash promise threatens her honour, every man in the story outdoes the others in generosity.

The Pardoner, a church official selling indulgences, cheerfully confesses his fraud: his relics are pigs' bones, his only text is 'Greed is the root of all evil', and he preaches it to make money. Then he tells a perfect moral tale. Three drunken rioters in plague-time Flanders set out to kill Death. An old man directs them to an oak tree, where they find a heap of gold. The youngest fetches wine and poisons it; the other two stab him on his return, drink, and die. Then the Pardoner tries to sell relics to the pilgrims, and the Host explodes.

cards.t: A rooster, a fox and Chaucer's flop
cards.b: The Knight makes peace between the Pardoner and the Host, and the tales roll on. The Prioress tells a pious, troubling legend of a Christian boy murdered by Jews. Chaucer himself, asked for a tale, recites the jingling romance of Sir Thopas until the Host stops him as worthless rhyming, so he switches to a long prose treatise. The Monk drones through tragedies until the Knight cuts him off. Then the Nun's Priest delights everyone with Chauntecleer, a vain rooster who ignores his dream, is flattered by a fox named Russell, captured, and talks his way free.

cards.t: The Parson closes, short of Canterbury
cards.b: As the journey nears its end, the Second Nun tells of Saint Cecilia, the Canon's Yeoman exposes his master's alchemical swindles, and the Manciple tells of a crow punished for speaking the truth. Then, as the sun sinks and a village near Canterbury comes into sight, the Host calls on the Parson for the last tale. He refuses to tell fables. Instead he delivers a long prose sermon on penitence and the seven deadly sins, turning the pilgrimage to Canterbury into a picture of the soul's journey to the heavenly Jerusalem.

The book ends with Chaucer's Retraction, in which he asks Christ's mercy and takes back those of his works, including 'the tales of Caunterbury' that lean towards sin, keeping only his devotional writings. We never see the pilgrims reach the shrine, never return to the Tabard, and never learn who wins the supper. Chaucer died in 1400 with only twenty-four tales written of the more than a hundred promised, some left broken off. Yet the incompleteness feels right: the journey, the arguments and the company were always the point.

cards.t: The Wife of Bath: experience talks back
cards.b: Alisoun is gap-toothed, deaf in one ear, dressed in scarlet stockings and a hat as broad as a shield, and the most alive person in medieval literature. She quotes Scripture to win arguments against it, celebrates desire without shame, and turns centuries of anti-women writing back on its authors. Chaucer lets her be funny, greedy and contradictory, which is exactly why she feels real.

The Pardoner is Chaucer's most unsettling creation. With his long yellow hair, goat-like voice and box of fake relics, he boasts that he preaches against greed purely to feed his own. Yet his tale of the three rioters is one of the most powerful moral stories ever written. He proves that a sermon can be true even when the preacher is rotten, and then, unbelievably, he tries his act on his audience.

cards.t: Chaucer the pilgrim: the innocent eye
cards.b: Our narrator is a plump, shy, seemingly naive man who admires almost everyone he meets. He calls the corrupt Monk a fine fellow and agrees he should not study. That innocence is a mask. By reporting without judging, Chaucer the poet lets readers see the satire for themselves, and by giving himself the worst tale on the road, he jokes at his own expense.

Pilgrims tell tales to 'quite', to pay one another back: Miller against Reeve, Friar against Summoner, Wife against every clerk who ever wrote about women. A story becomes an argument, an insult, a confession. And each tale reflects its teller: the Knight dreams of order, the Miller of appetite, the Pardoner of power over gullible people. Chaucer invented the idea that how you tell a story is who you are.

The pilgrimage is a religious journey, yet the Church's own people are its worst travellers. The Monk hunts, the Friar seduces and flatters, the Summoner takes bribes, the Pardoner sells pigs' bones as saints' relics. Against them stand the poor Parson, who 'first he wroghte, and afterward he taughte', and the Plowman. Chaucer's satire is not anti-faith; it measures religion by how people live it.

The Wife of Bath sets off a running debate. The Clerk answers with Griselda's total obedience, the Merchant with bitter cynicism about wives, and the Franklin with a marriage of equals where neither partner insists on mastery. Chaucer gives no final ruling, but the warmest answer comes from the Franklin and from the loathly lady: love thrives when power is shared rather than seized.

The Miller meant to mock carpenters and revealed his own drunken spite; the Reeve took the bait and exposed his bitterness. Whenever you tell a story about someone else, at work, at dinner, online, you are also telling one about yourself: what you notice, what you find funny, whom you resent. Before you tell it, ask what it says about the teller.

cards.t: Watch the gap between words and deeds
cards.b: The Pardoner preaches brilliantly against greed while picking his listeners' pockets, and the Parson preaches less eloquently but lives what he teaches. Fine words are cheap; consistency is rare. When you judge a leader, a colleague or yourself, look less at the speeches and more at the habits, which is exactly how Chaucer tells his good pilgrims from his bad ones.

The Wife of Bath has read few books, yet her five marriages give her arguments the scholars cannot answer. She reminds us that expertise is not only found in credentials. When someone tells you what they have actually lived through, about their job, body or family, give it real weight, even when it contradicts what the official sources say.

cards.t: Greed is a road that ends in death
cards.b: The three rioters set out to kill Death and find gold instead, and the gold becomes their death within hours, because each one wants it all. Chaucer's point is sharp: greed does not just corrupt, it isolates, turning friends into rivals. When money or credit enters a partnership, make the sharing explicit early, before suspicion has time to grow.

cards.t: Beware the flatterer at the gate
cards.b: Chauntecleer is caught not by force but by a fox praising his beautiful singing; he closes his eyes to crow and is seized. Then he escapes the same way, by flattering the fox into opening his mouth. When praise arrives just as someone wants something from you, keep your eyes open, and remember that a well-chosen word can also get you out of trouble.

In the Franklin's Tale, Arveragus lets Dorigen keep her rash promise; moved, the squire Aurelius releases her; moved again, the magician forgives Aurelius his debt. One act of decency triggers another. When a conflict seems locked, someone has to go first with a generous gesture. It may cost you, but it often frees everyone else to be better too.

The pilgrims insult and needle each other constantly, yet the journey continues because the Host keeps the game going and the Knight steps in to make the Pardoner and the Host kiss and make up. Any team, family or community will quarrel. What matters is having people willing to cool tempers, restore the rules and keep everyone moving down the same road.

Chaucer's pilgrims are strangers who would never otherwise share a table: a knight and a miller, a nun and a cook, a widow and a scholar. On the road, they listen to one another, laugh, argue and keep riding together. Who is the person in your life you would least expect to share a journey with, and what story might you hear if you asked them for one?
If you remember nothing else, remember this:

pts.h: Ideas have consequences
pts.d: Ivan's clever theory that "everything is permitted" is carried out, literally, by Smerdyakov with a heavy paperweight.

pts.h: We are each responsible for all
pts.d: Zosima, his brother Markel and finally Dmitri discover that guilt and love are shared, not neatly divided.

pts.h: Faith cannot be proved, only lived
pts.d: Ivan's arguments about suffering children go unanswered in words; Zosima and Alyosha answer them with deeds.

pts.h: A good memory can save a life
pts.d: Alyosha's speech at Ilyusha's stone argues that one remembered kindness can hold a person back from evil.

cards.t: A family that should not exist
cards.b: Russia, the 1860s, a few years after the serfs were freed, in a sleepy provincial town Dostoevsky calls Skotoprigonyevsk, roughly "Cattle-Pen-Ville".
