Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov is a rich, drunken, lecherous landowner and professional buffoon who abandoned his three sons to servants and relatives. Dmitri, the hot-blooded army officer, is the son of his first wife; Ivan, the cold intellectual, and Alyosha, the gentle novice monk, are sons of his second. A fourth, unacknowledged son lurks in the kitchen: Smerdyakov, the epileptic cook, said to be Fyodor's child by a homeless holy fool, Stinking Lizaveta.

cards.t: A scandal in the elder's cell
cards.b: The family gathers at the local monastery, supposedly so that the revered elder Zosima, Alyosha's spiritual father, can settle a quarrel between Dmitri and Fyodor over Dmitri's inheritance. Instead Fyodor clowns, insults the monks and lies outrageously; Dmitri arrives late and erupts in rage. Ivan's article on church and state is discussed, and his liberal relative Miusov reports Ivan's notorious idea: without God and immortality, everything is permitted. Then the dying Zosima does something baffling. He kneels and bows to the ground at Dmitri's feet, as if foreseeing some immense suffering ahead of him.

Dmitri pours out his heart to Alyosha in a ruined summer-house, reciting Schiller between swigs of brandy. Years ago, he says, the proud Katerina Ivanovna came alone to his rooms to beg money to save her father from disgrace; he gave her 4,500 roubles and let her go untouched, with a deep bow. Now they are engaged. But she trusted him with 3,000 roubles to post to Moscow, and he spent it carousing with Grushenka, a kept woman with whom he is madly in love. Worse, his own father also lusts after Grushenka, and has 3,000 roubles waiting in an envelope for her.

cards.t: Two women and a broken father
cards.b: Alyosha witnesses a shattering scene: Katerina, all generosity, kisses Grushenka's hand, believing she has won her rival over, only for Grushenka to refuse to kiss hers back and laugh in her face. The same evening Dmitri bursts into his father's house hunting for Grushenka, knocks the old man to the floor and kicks him in the face, shouting that he will come back and kill him. Zosima, sensing his death is near, orders Alyosha to leave the monastery after he dies and live in the world, among his troubled brothers.

cards.t: The captain who trampled the money
cards.b: Alyosha is sent on an errand of mercy. Dmitri has publicly dragged a poor, half-mad retired captain, Snegiryov, out of a tavern by his beard, while the captain's small son Ilyusha begged the jeering crowd to stop. Ilyusha, ill and ashamed, has since bitten Alyosha's finger to the bone. Katerina sends 200 roubles to make amends. Snegiryov, living in one squalid room with a crippled wife and daughters, is overjoyed by the money, then, suddenly remembering his son's honour, crumples the notes and grinds them into the sand with his heel.

In a tavern, Ivan finally talks openly with Alyosha. He does not deny God, he says; he refuses God's world. He has collected true stories of tortured children: a little girl locked in a freezing outhouse by her parents, a boy torn apart by a general's hounds before his mother's eyes. No future harmony, no heavenly forgiveness, can be worth one child's tears, and he will not accept a paradise bought at that price. Alyosha, shaken, admits that the general should be shot, and then reminds Ivan that there is One who can forgive everything.

cards.q: It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha, only I most respectfully return Him the ticket.
cards.b: This is the novel's hinge, from Constance Garnett's translation. Ivan is too honest to call suffering good and too proud to accept harmony on God's terms. Everything that follows, from the Grand Inquisitor to the murder, tests whether a mind that returns its ticket can still live, love, and stop others doing harm.

Ivan then recites a prose poem he has invented. Christ returns to sixteenth-century Seville, heals the sick and raises a dead child, and is promptly arrested by the ninety-year-old Grand Inquisitor. At night the old cardinal visits his cell and accuses him: by refusing Satan's three temptations, Christ offered humanity a freedom it is too weak to bear. The Church has corrected his work, giving people miracle, mystery and authority, bread and obedience instead. Christ says nothing. He simply kisses the old man on the lips. Alyosha, in turn, kisses Ivan.

cards.t: A servant's hint, a saint's death
cards.b: At the gate, Smerdyakov, who worships Ivan's ideas, hints slyly that Ivan should leave town: Dmitri knows the secret knocks that open Fyodor's door, and Smerdyakov may have a fit. Ivan understands enough to feel sick, but leaves for Moscow anyway. Meanwhile Zosima dies, after a final talk recorded by Alyosha: his dying brother Markel, who taught that each of us is guilty before all; his own youth as an officer who refused to fire in a duel; and a stranger who confessed to a hidden murder. Love everything, Zosima teaches, and be responsible for all.

cards.t: The smell of corruption, the onion
cards.b: The town expects a miracle, an incorrupt saint's body. Instead Zosima's corpse begins to smell within hours, and his enemies in the monastery gloat. Alyosha, scandalised by God's apparent insult to the holiest man he knew, lets the cynical seminarian Rakitin take him to Grushenka's house. But Grushenka, hearing of his grief, gently climbs off his lap, and they exchange kindness. She tells a folk tale about a wicked woman almost saved from hell by one onion she once gave away. Back at the coffin, Alyosha dreams of Cana, runs outside and kisses the earth.

Desperate to repay Katerina and win Grushenka, Dmitri spends a frantic day hunting 3,000 roubles: from Grushenka's old protector Samsonov, from a drunk timber dealer, from the gushing Madame Khokhlakova, who recommends gold mines. When Grushenka slips away, he seizes a brass pestle and runs to his father's garden. Through the window he sees the old man alone, waiting for her, and is overwhelmed by loathing. Something stops him. As he climbs back over the fence, the servant Grigory grabs his leg; Dmitri strikes him down with the pestle and flees, hands drenched with blood.

Dmitri learns that Grushenka has gone to the village of Mokroye to meet her first lover, a Polish officer who abandoned her years ago. Suddenly flush with cash, he buys champagne and food and races after her, planning to shoot himself at dawn. At the inn the Pole and his companion are caught cheating at cards and locked out; Grushenka realises it is Dmitri she loves. In the middle of their joy, police arrive. Fyodor has been found murdered, his skull smashed, the envelope torn open and empty. Every clue points at Dmitri.

Under interrogation, Dmitri tells the truth, which sounds like lies: he did not kill his father. The money came from Katerina's 3,000; he spent only 1,500 at Mokroye and kept the rest sewn in a rag around his neck, a shameful secret more painful to him than the charge of murder. Dozing between questions, he dreams of a burned-out village and a starving peasant mother with a crying baby. Waking, he wants to suffer for everyone so no babe need weep, accepts his ordeal, and is taken to prison.

Two months pass. Alyosha befriends the schoolboys who tormented Ilyusha, now dying, and wins over the precocious young radical Kolya Krasotkin. Ivan, returned and tormented, visits Smerdyakov three times. On the last visit the servant pulls 3,000 roubles out of his stocking and confesses calmly: he faked a fit, killed Fyodor with a cast-iron paperweight and took the money, all because Ivan had taught him that everything is permitted and had tacitly consented by leaving town. That night Smerdyakov hangs himself, and Ivan, feverish, receives a shabby gentleman devil.

The trial becomes a national sensation. Ivan stumbles into court, produces the money and says Smerdyakov did it, then raves about the devil and is carried out. Katerina, to save Ivan, whom she now loves, produces a drunken letter in which Dmitri promised to kill his father. The prosecutor paints a portrait of the reckless Karamazov soul; the brilliant defence lawyer argues there may have been no robbery at all, and that such a father was hardly a father. The peasant jurors are unmoved. Guilty, without mercy: twenty years' penal servitude in Siberia.

An escape to America is planned for Dmitri and Grushenka. Katerina visits Dmitri in the hospital; for a moment they confess they will always love each other. Ivan lies delirious. Then little Ilyusha dies, and after the funeral Alyosha gathers the twelve boys at a big stone where Ilyusha wanted to be buried. Whatever becomes of us, he tells them, let us never forget this day, this boy, and how good we felt together; one good memory can save a person. The boys shout, "Hurrah for Karamazov!" and go off hand in hand.

Dmitri is the Karamazov passions in their purest form: generous, violent, sentimental, ashamed. He says the ideal of the Madonna and the ideal of Sodom live side by side in him. Yet his deepest sense of honour is real; he would rather be called a murderer than a thief. Wrongly convicted, he becomes the novel's proof that suffering can remake a man from inside.

cards.t: Ivan: the mind that cannot rest
cards.b: Ivan is brilliant, proud and painfully honest, and his rebellion against a God who permits tortured children remains one of literature's strongest. But his ideas escape his control. Smerdyakov acts on them, and Ivan must face the possibility that he willed his father's death. His breakdown shows a conscience refusing to be silenced by its own arguments.

Alyosha, the youngest, is the hero Dostoevsky names in his preface: not a plaster saint but a cheerful, curious young man who listens. He doubts when Zosima's body smells, and recovers through Grushenka's kindness. He never wins an argument with Ivan; instead he goes to Snegiryov, the boys, his brothers, and quietly holds a broken family together.

The Grand Inquisitor claims people want bread and authority, not freedom, and that loving them means taking their freedom away. Dostoevsky lets the argument stand at full strength. His answer is not a rebuttal but Christ's silent kiss and Zosima's life: freely chosen love, which is harder than obedience and the only kind that counts.

Smerdyakov struck the blow, but the novel spreads the guilt wide. Dmitri wished his father dead and said so; Ivan supplied the philosophy and walked away; Fyodor himself bred hatred in sons he never raised. Zosima's teaching, that each of us is responsible for all, turns a detective puzzle into a question about the whole family, and the reader.

cards.t: Fathers, sons and the family's ruin
cards.b: The book is about what happens when a father abdicates. Fyodor's neglect produces four sons who are all, in some sense, orphans. Against him Dostoevsky sets other fathers: Zosima, spiritual father to Alyosha; Snegiryov, ridiculous but devoted to Ilyusha; and finally Alyosha, becoming a kind of father to the boys at the stone.

cards.t: Watch what your ideas permit others
cards.b: Ivan tosses off "everything is permitted" as a philosophical provocation; Smerdyakov hears it as a licence. Things we say casually to impress, about rules not mattering or certain people deserving harm, can land in a listener who takes them literally. Before you voice a clever, cynical idea, ask who might act on it.

cards.t: Pride can make you refuse help
cards.b: Snegiryov needs those 200 roubles desperately, yet he tramples them because accepting would feel like selling his son's honour. Alyosha understands and returns later, more gently, as an equal. When helping someone, protect their dignity; and when you are helped, ask whether your pride is costing those you love.

Katerina's kindnesses are real, but she uses them to keep score; she wants Dmitri bound by gratitude, and she kisses Grushenka's hand to master her. When generosity is meant to make someone owe you, it breeds resentment. The test of a gift is whether you are content if it is never repaid.

Ivan tells himself he did nothing; he merely went to Moscow. Smerdyakov, chillingly, shows him that his departure was a signal. Walking away from a situation you suspect will go wrong, at work, in a family, in a friendship, is a decision with consequences. Not acting is still acting.

Grushenka's onion story says one good deed may be enough to pull a soul out of hell. Her own kindness to grieving Alyosha does exactly that for him, and his for her. Don't wait to be a saint before being kind; the small gesture made today may be the one somebody remembers.

When Zosima's body decays, Alyosha's faith collapses into bitter disappointment, and yet that night he has his deepest spiritual experience. Crises of belief, in a person, cause or God, are not proof you were wrong to believe. Sometimes they burn away expectations so a sturdier love can grow.

Alyosha tells the boys that one bright memory from childhood can keep a person from evil years later. Fyodor gave his sons none, and see the result. Spend time deliberately making good shared memories with children, friends and family; they are moral capital that will be drawn on when you're not there.

Zosima teaches that each of us is responsible to all, for all. It sounds impossible, even unfair: how can I be responsible for a murder in a town I never visited? Yet the novel suggests that a cold word, a door left open or a child left unloved feeds the world's cruelty. Where is one place today where you could take responsibility you have been quietly avoiding?
